short_description: Biopsy thyroid, percutaneous core needle Notes: (If imaging guidance is performed, see 76942, 77002, 77012, 77021) (For fine needle aspiration biopsy, see 10004, 10005, 10006, 10007, 10008, 10009, 10010, 10011, 10012, 10021) (For evaluation of fine needle aspirate, see 88172, 88173)
lay_term: This is a diagnostic procedure in which the provider removes a tissue sample from the thyroid gland, typically under imaging guidance, using an automatic, spring–powered core needle. Explanation After the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider identifies the part of the thyroid to be investigated, typically under ultrasound guidance, which you can report separately. He then places the percutaneous core needle over the identified area. The core needle is a spring–powered device with a hollow inner needle that automatically moves in to scoop the thyroid tissue. The outer casing simultaneously follows to cut across the scooped tissue. The provider then pulls back the needle and sends the contents for pathological investigation. The provider typically performs this procedure to confirm a thyroid nodule as malignant or benign. Terminology Biopsy: Removal of a sample of tissue to investigate the associated organ of a suspected pathology. Core needle: An automatic spring–powered device with a hollow inner needle that moves in through the skin to scoop the tissue; the outer casing simultaneously follows to cut across the scooped tissue. Tips If the provider uses radiological guidance for the biopsy, choose the appropriate code based on the type of guidance used, such as 76942 for ultrasound, 77002 for fluoroscopy, 77012 for CT, or 77021 for MRI. Medicare allows practices to report 60100 once per lesion or nodule. For instance, if the provider performs biopsies on two nodules in the same lobe you should report 60100 twice. Providers may refer to a core needle biopsy as a percutaneous needle biopsy or PNB. Distinguishing fine needle aspiration, or FNA, from PNB can be confusing. One helpful tip is to associate fluid or cell sampling with FNA and associate core or tissue sampling with PNB. Read Less

short_description: Partial thyroid lobectomy, unilateral; with or without isthmusectomy
lay_term: This is a procedure involving surgical removal of a part of one of the two lobes the thyroid gland is divided into. The provider may perform the procedure with or without surgical removal of the isthmus, the tissue connecting the two lobes of the thyroid gland in the middle. Explanation After the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a standard neck incision about 3–5 inches horizontally in the lower part of the front of the neck just below the voice box. He separates the skin into upper and lower flaps and divides the overlying muscles. He takes care to avoid injury to the adjacent recurrent laryngeal nerve that innervates the vocal cord and to the overlying thyroid arteries and veins that provide blood circulation to the thyroid. He then removes a part of the lobe of the thyroid gland. He may or may not remove the isthmus as indicated. After achieving hemostasis, which is stoppage of bleeding, he closes the overlying muscles and skin in layers. A typical case involves removing a small localized benign nodule in an enlarged overactive thyroid in a patient with hyperthyroidism. Terminology Isthmusectomy: Surgical removal of the tissue connecting the two lobes of the thyroid gland in the middle. Partial thyroid lobectomy: Surgical removal of a part of a lobe of the thyroid gland. Unilateral: Of one side only; generally applied to structures symmetrically situated/duplicated in the left and the right halves of the human body. Read Less

short_description: Partial thyroid lobectomy, unilateral; with contralateral subtotal lobectomy, including isthmusectomy
lay_term: The procedure involves surgical removal of a part of one lobe of the thyroid gland and most of the portion of the other lobe of the thyroid gland. The provider also performs surgical removal of the isthmus, the tissue connecting the two lobes of the thyroid gland in the middle. Explanation After the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a standard neck incision about 3–5 inches horizontally in the lower part of the front of the neck just below the voice box. He separates the skin into upper and lower flaps and divides the overlying muscles. He takes care to avoid injury to the adjacent recurrent laryngeal nerve that innervates the vocal cord and to the overlying thyroid arteries and veins that provide blood circulation to the thyroid. He then removes only a part of the lesser affected lobe of the thyroid gland and removes most of the opposite lobe including the isthmus, too. After achieving hemostasis, which is stoppage of bleeding, he closes the overlying muscles and skin in layers. The provider typically performs this procedure to remove malignant cancerous tissue as in follicular adenomas or Hurthle cell tumors. The provider may also perform the procedure in patients with hot and cold nodules in an enlarged overactive thyroid in hyperthyroidism. Terminology Contralateral: The opposite side of the body from the area of primary focus. Isthmusectomy: Surgical removal of the tissue connecting the two lobes of the thyroid gland in the middle. Partial thyroid lobectomy: Surgical removal of a part of a lobe of the thyroid gland. Subtotal lobectomy: Surgical removal of most of one of the two lobes the thyroid gland is divided into. Thyroid: A gland in the neck that secretes hormones regulating growth and development. Unilateral: Of one side only; generally applied to structures symmetrically situated/duplicated in the left and the right halves of the human body. Tips Multiple codes apply to thyroid lobectomies: 60210, 60212, 60220, and 60225. Choose the appropriate code based on the extent of the gland excised. The thyroid has two lobes, so do not make the common mistake of referring to excision of a complete lobe as total thyroidectomy. Use 60210 when the provider excises only a part of one thyroid lobe, known as partial lobectomy. Report 60212 when the provider has removed part of one lobe and the greater portion of the other lobe simultaneously. Read Less

short_description: Total thyroid lobectomy, unilateral; with or without isthmusectomy
lay_term: This is a procedure involving complete surgical removal of one of the two lobes the thyroid gland is divided into. The provider may perform the procedure with or without surgical removal of the isthmus, the tissue connecting the two lobes of the thyroid gland in the middle. Explanation After the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a standard neck incision about 3–5 inches horizontally in the lower part of the front of the neck just below the voice box. He separates the skin into upper and lower flaps and divides the overlying muscles. He takes care to avoid injury to the adjacent recurrent laryngeal nerve that innervates the vocal cord and to the overlying thyroid arteries and veins that provide blood circulation to the thyroid. He then removes one complete lobe of the thyroid gland. He may or may not remove the isthmus as indicated. After achieving hemostasis, which is stoppage of bleeding, he closes the overlying muscles and skin in layers. The provider performs this procedure primarily to remove malignant cancerous thyroid tissue. Terminology Isthmusectomy: Surgical removal of the tissue connecting the two lobes of the thyroid gland in the middle. Total thyroid lobectomy: Complete surgical removal of a lobe of the thyroid gland. Unilateral: Of one side only; generally applied to structures symmetrically situated/duplicated in the left and the right halves of the human body. Tips When a provider discovers the need for a unilateral thyroid lobectomy during a parathyroidectomy, you may report both 60500 and 60220. You may need to append modifier 59 to 60500 depending on your payer’s edits. Multiple codes apply to thyroid lobectomies: 60210, 60212, 60220, and 60225. Choose the appropriate code based on the extent of the gland excised. The thyroid has two lobes, so do not make the common mistake of referring to excision of a complete lobe as total thyroidectomy. Report 60220 when the provider removes a complete lobe. If the provider also performs a subtotal lobectomy on the other side including isthmusectomy, report 60225. Read Less

short_description: Total thyroid lobectomy, unilateral; with contralateral subtotal lobectomy, including isthmusectomy
lay_term: The procedure involves surgical removal of one whole lobe of the thyroid gland and most of the other lobe of the thyroid gland. The provider also performs surgical removal of the isthmus, the tissue connecting the two lobes of the thyroid gland in the middle. Explanation After the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a standard neck incision about 3–5 inches horizontally in the lower part of the front of the neck just below the voice box. He separates the skin into upper and lower flaps and divides the overlying muscle, called the platysma, and separates the strap muscles from the midline. After gaining a view of the thyroid, he cuts and ties the ends of the overlying thyroid arteries and veins that provide blood circulation to the thyroid portion to be removed. He takes care to avoid injury to the adjacent recurrent laryngeal nerve that innervates the vocal cord. After slowly separating the thyroid from the underlying structures, he then removes one entire affected lobe of the thyroid gland and removes most of the opposite lobe including the isthmus, too. He spares the parathyroid gland. After achieving hemostasis, which is stoppage of bleeding, he closes the overlying muscles and skin in layers. The provider performs this procedure to remove tissue in malignant cancers and in an enlarged overactive thyroid in hyperthyroidism. Terminology Contralateral: The opposite side of the body from the area of primary focus. Isthmusectomy: Surgical removal of the tissue connecting the two lobes of the thyroid gland in the middle. Subtotal lobectomy: Surgical removal of most of one of the two lobes the thyroid gland is divided into. Unilateral: Of one side only; generally applied to structures symmetrically situated/duplicated in the left and the right halves of the human body. Tips Multiple codes apply to thyroid lobectomies: 60210, 60212, 60220, and 60225. Choose the appropriate code based on the extent of the gland excised. The thyroid has two lobes, so do not make the common mistake of referring to excision of a complete lobe as total thyroidectomy. Report 60225 when the provider removes a complete lobe and also performs a subtotal lobectomy on the other side including isthmusectomy. Read Less

lay_term: The procedure involves surgical removal of the entire thyroid gland. He separates the skin into upper and lower flaps and divides the overlying muscle, called the platysma, and separates the strap muscles from the midline. After gaining a view of the thyroid, he cuts and ties the ends of the overlying thyroid arteries and veins that provide blood circulation to the thyroid to be removed. short_description: Thyroidectomy, total or subtotal for malignancy; with limited neck dissection
lay_term: The procedure involves surgical removal of the entire thyroid or most of the thyroid, including the isthmus. The provider also performs limited lymph node dissection of the neck. Explanation After the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an extended neck incision based on factors like access, cosmetic appearance, and blood supply to the resultant flaps. He separates the skin into upper and lower flaps and divides the overlying muscles. After gaining a view of the thyroid, he cuts and ties the ends of the thyroid vessels that provide blood circulation to the thyroid and removes all or most of the thyroid. He takes care to avoid injury to the adjacent recurrent laryngeal nerve that innervates the vocal cord. He also removes neck structures including a limited number of lymph nodes of the neck. After achieving hemostasis, which is stoppage of bleeding, he closes the overlying muscles and skin in layers. The provider primarily performs this procedure to remove the thyroid and metastatic lymph nodes in the neck. Terminology Subtotal thyroidectomy: Surgical removal of most of the thyroid gland. Tips You may use 60252 for thyroidectomy with removal of nonmalignant lymph nodes as well as for malignant lymph node removal. The code describes malignancy for the thyroid and not for the lymph nodes per se. If the provider performed a radical neck dissection for the thyroid malignancy, report 60254. Read Less

short_description: Thyroidectomy, total or subtotal for malignancy; with radical neck dissection
lay_term: The procedure involves surgical removal of the entire thyroid or most of the thyroid, including the isthmus. The provider also performs neck dissection to remove neck structures extensively including malignant lymph nodes of the neck. Explanation After the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an extended neck incision based on factors like access, cosmetic appearance, and blood supply to the resultant flaps. He separates the skin into upper and lower flaps and divides the overlying muscles. After gaining a view of the thyroid, he cuts and ties the ends of the thyroid vessels that provide blood circulation to the thyroid and removes all or most of the thyroid. He takes care to avoid injury to the adjacent recurrent laryngeal nerve that innervates the vocal cord. He also removes neck structures including malignant cervical lymph nodes, greater auricular nerves, digastric muscle, stylohyoid muscle, spinal accessory nerve, internal jugular vein, and sternocleidomastoid muscle. After achieving hemostasis, which is stoppage of bleeding, he closes the overlying muscles and skin in layers. The provider primarily performs this procedure to remove extensive metastatic tissue in the neck including the cervical structures, lymph nodes, and the thyroid. Terminology Digastric muscle: Muscle used in lowering the jaw. Greater auricular nerves: Nerves supplying the skin around the ears. Internal jugular vein: A vein in the neck. Spinal accessory nerve: Nerve supplying the trapezius, a shoulder muscle. Sternocleidomastoid muscle: A muscle in the neck. Stylohyoid muscle: Muscle used in moving the hyoid bone. Subtotal: Surgical removal of most of the thyroid gland. Tips If the provider performed a limited neck dissection for the thyroid malignancy, report 60252. Read Less

After achieving hemostasis, which is stoppage of bleeding, he closes the overlying muscles and skin in layers. short_description: Thyroidectomy, including substernal thyroid; cervical approach
lay_term: The procedure involves surgical removal of the thyroid gland including its extension into the thorax below the sternum. Explanation After the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a standard neck incision about 3–5 inches horizontally in the lower part of the front of the neck just below the voice box. He separates the skin into upper and lower flaps and divides the overlying muscle, called the platysma, and separates the strap muscles from the midline. After gaining a view of the thyroid, he cuts and ties the ends of the overlying thyroid arteries and veins that provide blood circulation to the thyroid. He takes care to avoid injury to the adjacent recurrent laryngeal nerve that innervates the vocal cord. He slowly separates the thyroid from the underlying structures. He explores the substernal part of the gland through the thoracic inlet and gradually draws the thyroid up to the incised open area. He then removes the thyroid gland. He spares the parathyroid gland. After achieving hemostasis, which is stoppage of bleeding, he closes the overlying muscles and skin in layers. The provider primarily performs this procedure to remove malignant cancerous tissue or a larger goiter. Terminology Sternum: Also called the breastbone, a flat vertical long bone situated in the midline of the chest. Substernal thyroid: Thyroid gland formation extending down through the neck into the upper portion of the chest just behind the sternum. Thoracic inlet: A continuation or an opening from the neck into the chest through which all the vital structures like the wind pipe, the food pipe, and the blood vessels pass. Read Less

short_description: Excision of thyroglossal duct cyst or sinus
lay_term: The provider removes a thyroglossal duct cyst. A thyroglossal duct cyst is a cyst in the midline of the neck caused by a segment of the thyroglossal duct that did not close or disappear during embryonic development. The procedure is done to prevent infection, a recurrence of the cyst, or malignancy. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the region of the enlarged cyst. She then divides the surrounding muscles to free the cyst, and she ties and cuts the blood vessels. As the thyroglossal tract is closely associated with the hyoid bone, she cuts and removes the middle portion of the bone. Next, she incises a small cone of muscle from the base of the tongue to free the thyroglossal tract and removes the cyst and tract together. She repairs the tongue muscle, packs the wound, places a drain, and closes the incision. Terminology Hyoid bone: Small horseshoe–shaped bone located in the front of the neck, also called the lingual bone. Thyroglossal duct: A duct present during embryotic development that typically disappears once the thyroid gland is in its proper place. Thyroglossal sinus: An abnormal cavity or passage from the thyroglossal duct. Read Less

short_description: Excision of thyroglossal duct cyst or sinus; recurrent Notes: (For thyroid ultrasonography, use 76536)
lay_term: This procedure involves complete surgical removal of the thyroglossal duct cyst or sinus, including its full extent up to the back of the tongue as well as a portion of the hyoid bone. This is also known as the Sistrunk procedure. Recurrent cysts may appear when the patient’s infection was not under adequate control prior to previous surgery or when a previous surgery did not remove sufficient tissue. Explanation The provider first ensures that the infection is controlled with antibiotics. After the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a small transverse incision in front of the neck over the cyst. He separates the skin into upper and lower flaps. He then divides the overlying muscle called the platysma and separates the strap muscles from the midline and retracts them. He then isolates the cyst from the underlying tissues and removes it completely along with the tract following it up to the base of the tongue and removes it. He also cuts the middle portion of the hyoid bone, if present. He sends the tissue removed for pathological investigation. In case the previous provider did not remove the cyst and tract completely and the cyst has come back again or recurred, the current provider may have to remove a larger amount of tissue. After achieving hemostasis, which is stoppage of bleeding, he may place a drain and then close the overlying muscles and skin in layers. Terminology Thyroglossal duct: During embryonic development, the thyroid gland develops from the base of the tongue and moves down, leaving a connecting hollow tube known as a thyroglossal duct, which usually disappears as part of normal development. Thyroglossal duct cyst: This cyst results from accumulation of mucous fluid in a persistent thyroglossal duct; generally asymptomatic and identified as a soft swelling under the chin in the midline above the voice box; usually 1–3 cm in size and noticeable as one swallows. Thyroglossal duct sinus: An abnormal persistent drainage through an opening in the skin in front of the neck due to infection and subsequent rupture of a thyroglossal duct cyst through the skin. Tips Thyroglossal duct cysts are remnants of the embryonic duct that may occur anywhere from the base of the tongue to the thyroid gland. Seeing hyoid dissection in the documentation is one clue that 60281 is appropriate. Read Less

short_description: Parathyroidectomy or exploration of parathyroid(s)
lay_term: In the traditional procedure of parathyroid exploration, the provider surgically visualizes and screens the parathyroid glands for pathology based on their appearance and relative size. He may then perform parathyroidectomy, which is surgical removal of one or more parathyroid glands as indicated. The glands are a set of four small glands situated on the rear of the four corners of the butterfly shaped thyroid gland. Explanation After the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a standard neck incision about 3–5 inches horizontally in the lower part of the front of the neck just below the voice box. He separates the skin into upper and lower flaps and divides the overlying muscle, called the platysma, and separates the strap muscles from the midline. After gaining a view of the thyroid, he then pulls the thyroid back to gain a view of the parathyroid glands. He then identifies the pathological gland/glands, and to verify the diagnosis he may send a small piece for immediate pathological investigation. He may then remove the affected gland/glands while taking care to avoid injury to surrounding structures like blood vessels and the adjacent recurrent laryngeal nerve that innervates the vocal cord. After achieving hemostasis, which is stoppage of bleeding, he closes the overlying muscles and skin in layers. The provider primarily performs this procedure in primary hyperparathyroidism and parathyroid adenoma. Tips When a provider discovers the need for a unilateral thyroid lobectomy during a parathyroidectomy, you may report both 60500 and 60220. You may need to append modifier 59 to 60500 depending on your payer’s edits. Read Less

short_description: Parathyroidectomy or exploration of parathyroid(s); with mediastinal exploration, sternal split or transthoracic approach
lay_term: The provider examines or removes one or more of the parathyroid glands, the small endocrine glands, using one of three approaches. Providers typically perform this procedure to treat overactivity of the thyroid caused by a parathyroid adenoma. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises from the space at the base of the neck in between the two clavicle bones, down to the level of the space between the third and fourth rib for a sternal split incision. In a transthoracic approach, the provider incises through one or both sides of the chest. He exposes the thyroid and reexamines the parathyroid glands, especially those located in the mediastinal space. He identifies the parathyroid glands, and he isolates the adenoma and/or diseased gland or glands. He then removes any affected tissue and sends the surgical specimen to pathology for microscopic examination. Then he places a drain and closes the wound. Terminology Adenoma: Blood filled growth. Mediastinal: The space in the thoracic cavity between the lungs. Parathyroid glands: Glands located beneath the thyroid gland in the neck that secrete hormones, called parathormone or parathyrin, which regulate calcium and phosphorus metabolism by the body. Parathyroidectomy: Surgical procedure to remove the small endocrine glands that are adjacent to or embedded in the thyroid gland. Read Less

short_description: Parathyroid autotransplantation (List separately in addition to code for primary procedure) Notes: (Use 60512 in conjunction with 60500, 60502, 60505, 60212, 60225, 60240, 60252, 60254, 60260, 60270, 60271)
lay_term: Providers perform this procedure along with a primary procedure of thyroidectomy or parathyroidectomy. In this procedure, the provider takes the excised parathyroid tissue and places it into a muscle pocket either in the side of the neck or in the forearm muscles. The tissue develops a blood supply and starts working in 4 to 6 weeks. Explanation After the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a standard neck incision about 3–5 inches horizontally in the lower part of the front of the neck just below the voice box. He separates the skin into upper and lower flaps and divides the overlying muscle, called the platysma, and separates the strap muscles from the midline. After gaining a view of the thyroid, the provider may perform the separately reportable primary procedure of subtotal or total thyroidectomy or parathyroidectomy, depending on the patient’s needs. The primary procedure necessitates the removal of all parathyroids as well. Simultaneously, the provider cuts the excised parathyroid tissue into 1–2 mm fragments and places it in small pockets within the sternocleidomastoid muscle in the front of the neck or the forearm muscle. He then closes the muscle pocket with sutures. After achieving hemostasis, which is stoppage of bleeding, he closes the overlying muscles and skin in layers. The provider performs this procedure primarily to allow the patient’s body to secrete some parathyroid hormone for normal function after he removes all parathyroids. Terminology Parathyroid glands: Glands located beneath the thyroid gland in the neck that secrete hormones, called parathormone or parathyroid, which regulate calcium and phosphorus metabolism by the body. Parathyroidectomy: Surgical procedure to remove the small endocrine glands that are adjacent to or embedded in the thyroid gland. Tips Because +60512 is an add–on code, payers will not reimburse you if you report it without an appropriate primary code: 60212, 60225, 60240, 60252, 60254, 60260, 60270, 60271, 60500, 60502, and 60505. Codes 60200, 60210, and 60220 are not in the primary code list with add–on code +60512 as auto transplantation would typically not be necessary in unilateral procedures. If the provider performs this nevertheless, append modifier 22 to 60200, 60210, or 60220 to represent the increased service. Do not report +60512 as an add–on code if the transplant site is sternocleidomastoid and approached through the same neck incision. Read Less

short_description: Thymectomy, partial or total; sternal split or transthoracic approach, without radical mediastinal dissection (separate procedure)
lay_term: The provider removes a part or the entire thymus gland without removing adjacent structures. The procedure is often done as a result of a benign or malignant tumor on the thymus gland, called a thymoma. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a length–wise incision through the breast bone, or sternum, and the sternum is split vertically. In a transthoracic approach, the provider incises through one or both sides of the chest. She explores the chest and removes part of or the entire thymus gland without removing adjacent structures. She inspects the surgical field to ensure no residual thymic tissue remains and inserts chest tubes. She then closes the site in layers and applies a sterile dressing. Terminology Radical mediastinal dissection: Surgical removal of all lymphatics in the neck along with nonlymphatic structures including: sternocleidomastoid muscle, one of the muscles that functions to flex the head; internal jugular, neck vein; submandibular gland, one of the salivary glands, and the spinal accessory nerve, a nerve that helps control speech, swallowing and certain movements of the head and neck . Thymectomy: Surgical removal of the thymus gland. Thymus gland: Gland found in the base of the neck that is responsible for white blood cell development that is important for immune system response. short_description: Adrenalectomy, partial or complete, or exploration of adrenal gland with or without biopsy, transabdominal, lumbar or dorsal (separate procedure)
lay_term: The provider explores or removes one or both of the adrenal glands, which are two small organs located above the kidneys that secrete hormones to help regulate the immune system, metabolism, blood sugar levels, and blood pressure. The procedure covers different surgical approaches and biopsy when performed. The provider performs this procedure primarily to investigate or treat malignancy of the adrenal glands. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision based upon the tumor size, location, and invasiveness. The provider can perform the procedure through a transabdominal approach, which is incising across the abdomen; a lumbar approach, which is incising a vertical line from the armpit down to the top of the pelvis; or a dorsal approach, which is a curved flank incision, made over a rib. Once he gains access to the area, he explores the abdomen to identify the extent of disease. The provider may decide to biopsy suspicious sites and send them to pathology for immediate microscopic examination. He then isolates the adrenal glands and identifies any tumor or diseased gland or glands. He ties off the surrounding blood vessels of a diseased gland before removal to prevent excessive bleeding and then dissects the glands. He then releases and dissects the attached tissue of the gland from surrounding structures. He may remove one or both of the adrenal glands. If an adjacent retroperitoneal tumor is present, he carefully resects the mass along with a margin of uninvolved tissue. He removes it together with the adrenal gland and sends the specimen to pathology for examination. The provider rinses the abdominal cavity with a sterile saline solution, closes the wounds, and sutures the incisions. Terminology Adrenalectomy: Removal of one or both adrenal glands. Resect: To take out surgically. short_description: Puncture of shunt tubing or reservoir for aspiration or injection procedure Notes: (For radiological supervision and interpretation, use 75809)
lay_term: In this procedure, called a shunt tap, the provider inserts a needle into the tube of a shunt or its reservoir to withdraw cerebrospinal fluid, or CSF, or he injects a medication or other substance into the CSF. The provider performs this service to measure pressure, test the patency of the shunt device, meaning that it is open and unobstructed, aspirate fluid for diagnosis, or to inject medication or contrast. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider locates the shunt reservoir as a smooth dome under the skin. He may access the shunt tubing or the reservoir by inserting a needle perpendicular through the skin into the tubing, and or continuing to slowly advance it into the reservoir. If the flow is slow, then he may adjust the angle of the needle to facilitate the flow. If he acquires only a small amount of CSF, then the provider knows he has accessed the reservoir. But if it does not flow freely, then it may indicate an obstruction. He then checks the effectiveness of the drainage system by holding the end of the tubing below the level of the reservoir to see if CSF will fill the tube and begin to drip. If, however, CSF easily flows from the tube or reservoir, the provider may take a reading of the intraventricular pressure by holding the tubing vertically and using a manometer, a special tube that attaches to the needle to measure the pressure of the CSF. He may also administer a medication such as an antibiotic, or diagnostic agent such as contrast through the needle. He removes the needle, applies gentle pressure, and covers the site with a sterile dressing. Any CSF samples he acquires he sends to the laboratory for analysis. Terminology Aspiration: To withdraw fluid from a body cavity or a mass, e.g. a cyst, with a needle and a syringe. Cervical vertebrae: Seven vertebra located in the upper neck of the spinal column, the vertebral column, indicated by the symbols C1 through C7. Contrast: A special dye used in radiology imaging to improve the visibility of internal structures or organs of the body, which providers administer to patients through various routes, including oral and intravenously; also called contrast material, contrast medium, contrast media, contrast agent, or contrast dye. Intraventricular: Within a ventricle. Shunt: A narrow tube that allows excess cerebrospinal fluid, or CSF, that builds up inside the ventricles in the brain, to drain into another part of the body. Vertebrae: The bony segments that form the spine. There are 33 segments designated into 5 different levels: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral and 4 coccygeal. Tips Report a shunt tap even if it is within the shunt placement's global period. Read Less

Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a small scalp incision and moves the scalp away. Then she uses a manual twist drill at the incision site, which she cranks or twists by hand to perforate the skull and expose the dura mater, the tough outermost layer of the three protective layers that surround the brain and spinal cord. She then uses the hole to aspirate a sample of cerebrospinal fluid, or CSF, by inserting a needle through the hole to obtain a sample of fluid. Catheter: A flexible or rigid hollow tube placed into the body for administration of medication or fluids, to remove a fluid or to keep a passage open. Intracerebral: Front of the brain. Neuroendoscope: A small, tubular type instrument with a fiberoptic light source used to view the brain and spinal cord. Subdural: Beneath the outermost membrane covering the brain and spinal cord. Twist drill: Handheld and manually operated drill with one or more deep spiral grooves that extend from the point to the smooth part of the shaft. Ventricles: Chambers in the brain filled with cerebrospinal fluid, or CSF. short_description: Burr hole(s) with evacuation and/or drainage of hematoma, extradural or subdural Notes: (For bilateral procedure, report 61154 with modifier 50)
lay_term: The provider drills a hole or holes into the skull to drain or evacuate a hematoma, a collection of blood on the outside or underneath the dura of the brain. The service is done to access a hematoma that can occur as a result of trauma or a medical procedure. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider reviews prior radiologic images, usually a computed tomography, or CT, scan that identifies the hematoma. She then incises the scalp over the area of the hematoma and moves the scalp away to expose the bone. Next, she uses a surgical drill to create a burr hole or holes into the skull at the location of the hematoma. If she visualizes an extradural hematoma, she drains the epidural space. If it is a subdural hematoma, she incises the dura, and the blood drains. She then carefully places a catheter into either area to gently suction the remaining hematoma. She sends the liquid she collects through the catheter for laboratory testing. The provider then gently irrigates any remaining blood or clots and assesses the results of the surgery. She then removes the catheter, sutures the dura closed, and may replace the bone plug. She then reapproximates and sutures the scalp, then dresses the wound. If, however, sufficient drainage does not occur, she may leave the catheter in place for several days prior to its removal to ensure optimal drainage of the hematoma. Terminology Burr hole: Hole drilled into the skull using a burr drill, also called trepanation or trephination. Catheter: A flexible or rigid hollow tube placed into the body for administration of medication or fluids, to remove a fluid, or to keep a passage open. Computed tomography, or CT: Computed tomography, or CT, is when the provider rotates an X–ray tube and X–ray detectors around a patient, which produces a tomogram, a computer generated cross sectional image; providers use CT to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases. Epidural space: The space that surrounds the dura, which is the outermost layer that surrounds the spinal canal; the epidural space houses the spinal nerve roots, blood and lymphatic vessels, and fatty tissues. Extradural: Outside the dura, the tough outer membrane surrounding the central nervous system. Reapproximates: To align or rejoin tissue. Subdural space: The space under the dura mater, the outermost of the three membranes covering the brain. Tips Report radiologic imaging separately. Whenever you encounter the term burr hole while reading the operative report, distinguish between a burr hole the provider performs as a primary surgical approach versus those he makes in conjunction with a craniotomy. In a procedure commonly described as a bone flap craniotomy, a provider drills several burr holes to help develop a bone flap. If this is the case, the surgical approach is not a burr hole, but rather a craniotomy or craniectomy, and you should use the correct craniotomy or craniectomy code. Many of these codes include a parenthetical with the term describing a burr hole, having an "s" in parentheses, meaning burr hole or holes. The presence of the parentheses indicates that the provider should use these codes only once regardless of the number of burr holes necessary to perform the procedure at the specific location of the brain. Also, report these codes only once regardless of the side or number of burr holes involved at a specific location or for a specific lesion. When a burr hole or holes is medically necessary to perform procedures at a different anatomic location of the brain, a separate code identifying the burr hole and specific procedures the provider performs may be necessary. This often requires the use of a modifier in order to identify that a separate and distinct location was involved and documentation that supports the same. Read Less

short_description: Burr hole(s) or trephine, supratentorial, exploratory, not followed by other surgery Notes: (For bilateral procedure, report 61250 with modifier 50)
lay_term: The provider drills a burr hole or holes into the skull supratentorially, or above the tentorium, and inspects the brain. This procedure is generally done when other diagnostic testing is unable to determine the reason for a condition or the extent of a disorder. The provider does not at his time perform a surgical procedure subsequent to this service. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the scalp over the area to be explored and moves the scalp away to expose the bone. Next, she uses a surgical drill to create a burr hole or holes into the skull and exposes the brain. This action alone may be enough to release the presence of air or gas within the cranial cavity that may have been compressing the brain. She explores the supratentorial area for adverse underlying conditions, and when the provider completes her assessment, she sutures the dura if opened during exploration and may replace the bone plug. She then reapproximates and sutures the scalp, then dresses the wound. The provider does not perform a subsequent procedure during this service. short_description: Craniectomy or craniotomy for evacuation of hematoma, supratentorial; extradural or subdural
lay_term: Hematoma is an unusual collection of blood outside the blood vessels due to internal hemorrhage. Subdural or extradural hematoma is caused by head injuries, and it is a life–threatening condition. These hematomas can be removed through suction, for which the physician has to perform an incision of the scalp, craniotomy, or craniectomy. A supratentorial hematoma is the accumulation of blood in the region above the tentorium cerebella (or the cerebellar tentorium –– the extended dura mater that surrounds and separates the cerebellum from the other parts of brain in the posterior cerebral hemisphere). Explanation After confirmation of the presence of a subdural or extradural hematoma through a CT scan, the patient is made to lie in park bench position. A trephine margin is made, a linear paramedian incision is made, and the muscle and fascia are retracted. The physician performs a craniotomy (drills holes through the cranium) with a skull trephine craniotome, or craniectomy (surgically removes a part of the skull bone) to access the hematoma. Using direct visualization, the physician uses suction devices to suck the hematoma out. Next, she drills burr holes in the skull. She inserts a surgical saw, called a craniotome, through the burr holes, and cuts between adjacent burr holes to create a bone flap, which she removes to expose the dura. The provider opens the dura and exposes the swollen brain. She excises and removes a sufficient portion of the lobe to reduce the ICP. After adequate pressure reduction and thorough control of bleeding, she closes the dura with sutures or a graft to allow for expansion. short_description: Other cranial decompression, posterior fossa Notes: (For orbital decompression by lateral wall approach, Kroenlein type, use 67445)

lay_term: In this procedure, the provider partially or totally removes a brain lobe, other than the temporal lobe, such as the frontal, parietal, or occipital lobe, through an elevated portion of skull bone. The provider also performs an intraoperative electrocorticography (ECoG) to record the electrical activity in the brain and pinpoint the site of seizures. This procedure helps define the area in the brain where epileptic seizures begin. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the scalp and creates burr holes to elevate a portion of skull bone. He then retracts the brain membranes to access the affected lobe of the brain. Then he places electrodes on the surface of the brain over the first layer of membrane protecting the brain. He may also place depth electrodes into deep areas of the brain using very thin wires. Next, he connects the electrodes to continuous electroencephalogram, or EEG, equipment. He records and maps the activity, moving the electrodes as necessary to gather data. He uses the resulting information to define the extent of the brain causing the seizures, and he identifies critical areas to avoid. He then partially or totally removes the lobe. The provider then drains out any excess fluid or blood using a drain. After the removal of the lesion or area of brain abnormality, he uses the electrocorticography (ECoG) again to determine if any residual epileptic activity remains. When he obtains the result he desires, he removes the electrodes and sutures the layers of membranes. Finally, he attaches the bone flap back to its original position using plates, wires, or sutures, sutures the layers of tissue together, and he covers the wound with a sterile dressing. short_description: Surgery of complex intracranial aneurysm, intracranial approach; carotid circulation
lay_term: The provider treats a complex intracranial aneurysm using an intracranial surgical technique to repair an abnormal dilation, or widening, of a blood vessel in the internal carotid circulation. This service helps treat an aneurysm that a subarachnoid hemorrhage causes. Explanation A complex intracranial aneurysm is usually large, typically larger than 1.5 cm, or 15 mm, or in areas of the brain that are difficult to access. They may have arterial trunks and branches that are part of the aneurysm and may have a calcified or complex wall structure. A provider also considers an intracranial aneurysm as complex if vessel occlusion, trapping, or cardiopulmonary bypass is necessary during the procedure. The ultimate goal of the procedure is to exclude the aneurysm from the cerebral circulation while trying to preserve the blood flow, with minimal brain dissection and retraction, if possible. The surgical technique the provider uses depends upon the location and complexity of the brain aneurysm. The provider performs an angiogram prior to this procedure to identify the location of the aneurysm. In an intracranial approach to a complex carotid vessel aneurysm, the provider incises the scalp over the area of the aneurysm. He then retracts the scalp to expose the bone. Next, he uses a surgical drill to create a burr hole, or pattern of burr holes in the skull. He inserts a surgical saw, called a craniotome, through the burr holes and cuts between adjacent burr holes to create a bone flap, which he removes to expose the dura, the thick outer protective layer covering the brain. The provider incises the dura and exposes the underlying brain. He then carefully dissects down to expose the aneurysm, exposing the vessels and identifying the neck of the aneurysm. He may use temporary occlusion clips as he dissects vessels that are part of the neck of the aneurysm. When he fully exposes the neck, he may use different techniques to treat the aneurysm. For many aneurysms, he clips the neck of the aneurysm but is careful to exclude adjacent vessels. If the provider finds a calcified wall structure, he may need to incise and suture the aneurysm. Where other critical vessels arise from the aneurysm, he may need to maintain blood flow, so he bypasses the aneurysm first before occluding it. He may also need to place the patient on cardiac bypass equipment to stop the patient’s heart and allow for dissection of the limp aneurysm from the brain. Or he may temporarily occlude, or block, the aneurysm to decompress it. Regardless of the surgical approach or additional procedure that he performs, he obtains hemostasis at the end of the procedure and checks the trapping, resection, or bypass repair of the vessel. When he is satisfied, he closes the dura and replaces and secures the bone flap. Before closing the scalp, he may place a drain and then reapproximates the tissue layers, closes the scalp, and applies sterile dressings. Terminology Aneurysm: An abnormal dilation, or widening, of a blood vessel due to weakness of the wall. Angiography: A medical imaging technique used to visualize the lumen, or inside, of blood vessels and organs of the body ; an angiogram is a record of the image. Burr hole: Hole drilled into the skull using a burr drill. Carotid circulation: The carotid circulation supplies oxygen and vital nutrients to the anterior, or front part, of the brain. Hemostasis: The stoppage of blood flow. Intracranial: Within the skull on or in the brain. Reapproximates: To align or rejoin tissue. Resection: Surgical incision of all or part of an organ, tissue, or structure. Subarachnoid hemorrhage: Bleeding in the area between the brain and the thin tissues that cover the brain. Vertebrobasilar circulation: The vascular network that supplies blood to the back part of the cerebral hemispheres; also known as a posterior circulation; created by the two vertebral arteries that arise from the spinal column and join in the brain to form the basilar artery, also called the vertebrobasilar artery. He may use temporary occlusion clips as he dissects vessels that are part of the neck of the aneurysm. When he fully exposes the neck, he may use different techniques to resolve the aneurysm. For many aneurysms, he clips the neck of the aneurysm but is careful to exclude adjacent vessels. If the provider finds a calcified wall structure, he may need to incise and suture the aneurysm. Where other critical vessels arise from the aneurysm, he may need to maintain blood flow, so he bypasses the aneurysm first before occluding it. He may also need to place the patient on cardiac bypass equipment to stop the patient’s heart and allow for dissection of the limp aneurysm from the brain. Or he may temporarily occlude, or block, the aneurysm to decompress it. Regardless of the surgical approach or additional procedure he performs, he obtains hemostasis at the end of the procedure and checks the trapping, resection, or bypass repair of the vessel. When he is satisfied, he closes the dura and replaces and secures the bone flap. Before closing the scalp, he may place a drain and then reapproximates the tissue layers, closes the scalp, and applies sterile dressings. lay_term: In this procedure, the provider removes a portion of skull bone to access an aneurysm, vascular malformation, or carotid–cavernous fistula. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the scalp to remove a portion of skull bone to access the aneurysm, vascular malformation, or carotid–cavernous fistula. He then embolizes the malformation, deliberately occluding the blood supply of the lesion by placing a small plastic particle, glue, metal coil, or balloon through the blood supply. The provider then drains out any excess fluid or blood using a drain, and he sutures the layers of dural tissue together. Finally, he attaches the bone flap back to its original position using plates, wires, or sutures, and he covers the wound with a sterile dressing. lay_term: In this procedure, the provider surgically connects, or anastomoses, the arterial and extracranial intracranial arteries, specifically the middle cerebral and cortical arteries. He accesses the arteries through a craniotomy, where he removes a portion of the skull bone. This procedure treats blockage and rupture of vessels in the brain by effectively bypassing the affected area to restore blood flow to the brain. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the scalp located above the affected arteries and retracts the scalp to expose the bone. Next, he uses a surgical drill to create a burr hole, or pattern of burr holes in the skull. He inserts a surgical saw, called a craniotome, through the burr holes and cuts between adjacent burr holes to create a bone flap, which he removes to expose the dura, the thick outer protective layer covering the brain. The provider incises the dura and exposes the intracranial site for anastomosis. Next, he carefully identifies the feeder branch, the donor vessel that will be used to bypass the blockage and the recipient artery, the vessel that the feeder will be connected to, that are suitable for bypass. Then he dissects these arteries from the surrounding tissue. Next, he places temporary clips on the donor and recipient vessels. He incises the donor and prepares the end. The provider then makes an opening in the side of the recipient vessel and sutures the feeder’s prepared end to the recipient artery. After he attaches the vessels, the provider releases the temporary clips and verifies there are no leaks, checks for good blood flow, and then achieves hemostasis. When he is satisfied, he closes the dura and replaces and secures the bone flap. Before closing the bone flap, he may enlarge an area to allow passage of the bypass vessel without kinking or pressure. lay_term: Medicare National Coverage Determinations Manual Cingulotomy is a psychosurgical procedure designed to interrupt the interconnecting neuronal pathways of the brain involved in the regulation of the emotions and certain autonomic functions. The intent of psychosurgery is to modify or alter disturbances of behavior, thought content, or mood that are not responsive to other conventional modes of therapy, or for which no organic pathological cause can be demonstrated by established methods. Explanation The operation usually involves bilateral lesions that are placed in the anterior cingulum of the brain. First, a scalp incision is made down to the bone, and a burr hole is made through the skull and enlarged as necessary. Next, a dural incision is made and a small dilating probe is inserted which gradually displaces the brain tissue along the guided straight line to the depth of the target point. Electrocautery probes are stereotactically inserted through lateral burr holes drilled in the skull. A radiofrequency pulsating current is used to ablate the tissue that connects the limbic system to the frontal lobe. Two or three repeat procedures may be performed in the same patient when a satisfactory result has not been achieved with the first cingulotomy. The surgeon provides the procedure under MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) guidance. After creating the lesion, the dura is sutured and scalp is closed. Terminology Stereotactic surgery or stereotaxy is a minimally invasive form of surgical intervention which makes use of a three–dimensional coordinates system to locate small targets inside the body and to perform on them some action such as ablation (removal), biopsy, lesion, injection, stimulation, implantation, radiosurgery (SRS), etc. Read Less

short_description: Stereotactic implantation of depth electrodes into the cerebrum for long-term seizure monitoring
lay_term: The provider implants depth electrodes into the cerebrum of the brain using three dimensional imaging to map the implant location. This procedure is done to identify the abnormal area of the brain causing a patient’s epileptic seizures. Explanation Prior to the procedure, the provider begins by taking computed tomography, CT, or magnetic resonance imaging, MRI, scans to locate the coordinates in the brain to place the electrodes. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the scalp and retracts the flap to expose the bone. Next, he makes a burr hole or holes in the skull raising a bone flap as necessary to access the site. He then incises the dura and carefully inserts a small probe, which gradually moves brain tissue away along its path to the target point identified by the CT or MRI mapped coordinates. He then places the intracerebral, or depth, electrodes, which are thin wire electrodes, in the brain. Next, he connects the electrodes to continuous electroencephalogram, or EEG, equipment to monitor the brain activity. Once the electrodes are in place, the provider continuously records activity both between events, known as interictal activity, and during seizures, or ictal activity. Using a computer, he analyzes these recordings to identify the point where the EEG activity begins before it spreads to adjacent areas. If he identifies a specific cortical area consistently at the onset, then that area is likely to be the seizure focal point, or where the seizure begins. When the procedure is complete, he replaces the bone flap, securing it with permanent plates, wires, and screws. He then folds the tissue flap back, closes the scalp, and places a sterile dressing over the area. Terminology Burr hole: Hole drilled into the skull using a burr drill, also called trepanation or trephination. Cerebrum: The frontal lobes of the brain. Computed tomography, or CT: Computed tomography, or CT, is when the provider rotates an X–ray tube and X–ray detectors around a patient, which produces a tomogram, a computer generated cross sectional image; providers use CT to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases. Intracranial EEG, or iEEG: Recording of electrical activity from the cerebral cortex of the brain by placing electrodes on the surface of the brain; also called electrocorticography, or ECoG. Electrodes: A conductor or small disc that attaches to the skin and detects tiny electrical charges; or brain activity. Intracerebral: Front of the brain. Magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI: Radiographic imaging using magnetic fields and radio waves to visualize body tissues to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases. Stereotactic: The creation of three dimensional coordinates to precisely locate a target site in the body and direct instrumentation or beam of radiation. Tips Whenever you encounter the term burr hole while reading the operative report, distinguish between a burr hole the provider performs as a primary surgical approach versus those he makes in conjunction with a craniotomy. In a procedure commonly described as a bone flap craniotomy, a provider drills several burr holes to help develop a bone flap. If this is the case, the surgical approach is not a burr hole, but rather a craniotomy or craniectomy, and you should use the correct craniotomy or craniectomy code. Many of these codes include a parenthetical with the term describing a burr hole, having an "s" in parentheses, meaning burr hole or holes. The presence of the parentheses indicates that the provider should use these codes only once regardless of the number of burr holes necessary to perform the procedure at the specific location of the brain. Also, report these codes only once regardless of the side or number of burr holes involved at a specific location or for a specific lesion. When a burr hole or holes is medically necessary to perform procedures at a different anatomic location of the brain, a separate code identifying the burr hole and specific procedures the provider performs may be necessary. This often requires the use of a modifier in order to identify that a separate and distinct location was involved and documentation that supports the same. Read Less

The targeted lesion is simple, which typically means the lesion’s maximum dimension is less than 3.5 cm. Explanation Prior to the procedure, the provider appropriately positions the patient and places fiducial markers, or imaging markers, on the patient's scalp, and or he places a stereotactic head frame on the patient. lay_term: In this procedure, the provider removes a portion of the skull, or he may create a twist drill or burr hole in a patient’s skull. He then uses a stereotactic method, which makes use of a three dimensional coordinate system to locate small targets inside the brain and places a neurostimulator electrode array on the targeted location in a subcortical site. In this procedure, the provider does not obtain an intraoperative microelectrode recording. The provider performs this service to treat chronic difficult to control tremors, dystonia, involuntary movements and muscle contractions, or Parkinson’s disease. Explanation Prior to the procedure, the provider appropriately positions the patient and places fiducial markers, or imaging markers, on the patient's scalp, and or he places a stereotactic head frame on the patient. He then works with radiology to identify and precisely image the target area using computed tomography, or CT, or magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, scans imported into a computer system that provides three dimensional images of the brain. The provider determines the coordinates for the target by measuring reference lines and calculating angles using a computer to determine various trajectories. He chooses the best entry point and trajectory to use through the scalp to pinpoint the target. After planning is complete, and the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider identifies the target area of the brain using the stereotactic method, in which previously taken CT or MRI images are imported into a computer system that provides three dimensional images of the brain. He locates the entry point, incises the scalp, and retracts the skin flap. Next, he makes a twist drill or burr hole in the skull or removes a larger portion of skull bone to access the identified target area and expose the dura. He then incises the dura and inserts electrode array protected in a cannula into the subcortical area, and using the computer, he carefully places the electrode array at the target location. The provider then tests the array, moving and repositioning the array as necessary until he discovers its optimal position. He ensures that the electrodes are correctly placed by stimulating the area to obtain tremor cessation, reduction in rigidity, and or mobility and coordination of a limb, with the least side effects from the electrode placement. He then removes the guide cannula and using imaging guidance, he anchors the array. He sutures the dura and obtains complete hemostasis before coiling the array lead in a pocket under the galea, the tough layer of dense fibrous tissue that covers the upper part of the skull. He then sutures the galea. He may replace the removed skull bone and then reapproximates the scalp and sutures or staples it closed. He applies sterile dressings to the wound. Stereotactic: The creation of three dimensional coordinates to precisely locate a target site in the body and direct instrumentation or beam of radiation. Stereotactic head frame: A device attached to the head that is used as a measuring guide to determine the coordinates for targeting an abnormality and to position the head for brain surgery. Trajectory: The route or movement of an object along a three dimensional path. lay_term: The provider implants a small neurostimulator pulse generator or receiver in the skull, under the scalp. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider begins the procedure to insert a skull–mounted cranial neurostimulator pulse generator or receiver. The provider makes an incision to access the skull at the desired location for the neurostimulator implant. The provider may then perform craniectomy or craniotomy. Craniectomy involves removing a piece of the skull, but the provider doesn’t immediately replace the bone. In a craniotomy, the provider temporarily removes a piece of the skull, called a bone flap, then replaces it after the brain surgery is completed. The provider implants the generator or receiver, attaching it to the skull. For instance, the provider may secure a sort of ring or band in the skull opening and secure the neurostimulator device in it so the implants sit flush with the skull and don’t protrude above the surface. The device may have direct or inductive coupling, which refers to the method of energy transfer from the power source to the device itself. Direct coupling in a neurostimulator device means the power source is directly connected to the device, such as through a wired connection. Inductive coupling, on the other hand, involves the transfer of energy from the power source to the device through a magnetic field. The provider may perform a test stimulation to ensure the system is functioning as desired. The provider then closes the access site. short_description: Elevation of depressed skull fracture; compound or comminuted, extradural
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider incises the scalp and elevates a depressed skull fracture, meaning a portion of skull bone moved inward into the brain. This service is for a compound or comminuted fracture that may involve a break in, or loss of, skin and the skull bone being broken into fragments, but the break does not reached the dura, the outer membrane covering the brain. The procedure corrects the noticeable depression in the skull to restore the normal appearance of the skull. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the scalp over the area of the depressed skull fracture. He then retracts the scalp to locate the depression. Next, the provider creates one or more burr holes outside the fractured area. Then he passes surgical instrumentation through the burr hole and carefully frees any dural adhesion and then lifts up the bony fragments to restore the anatomical position. He then stabilizes the bony parts in position using bone dust he preserves from the creation of the burr hole or other materials to fill the gaps between the fracture lines as necessary. Finally, he sutures the layers of scalp tissue together and covers the wound with a sterile dressing. Terminology Burr holes: Surgical drill used to create a hole or pattern of holes in the skull. Compound fracture: Break associated with an open wound or break is into a cavity that has opening to the outside, such as the sinuses; considered surgical emergencies due to risk of infection. Comminuted fracture: Break in which the skull bone is broken into many pieces and may or may not have an associated open wound. Epidural: Outer part of the spinal canal. Read Less

short_description: Elevation of depressed skull fracture; with repair of dura and/or debridement of brain
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider incises the scalp and elevates a depressed skull fracture, meaning a portion of skull bone moved inward into the brain. The provider also repairs the dura, the outer membrane covering the brain , and debrides the brain when necessary. The procedure reduces pressure on the brain and corrects the noticeable depression in the skull to restore the normal appearance of the skull. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the scalp over the area of the depressed skull fracture. He then retracts the scalp to locate the depression. Next, the provider creates one or more burr holes outside the fractured area. He elevates and removes the bony fragments and inspects the dura for tears. If he finds a tear, he repairs the dura and debrides the brain as necessary, being careful to maintain hemostasis to prevent postoperative blood collection in the skull. He soaks the bony fragments he removes in an antibiotic solution. He then reassembles the pieces, possibly wiring together the larger sections, or he may use a surgical mesh or other implant to cover the defect. Finally, he replaces the scalp over the area, sutures the layers of scalp tissue together, and then covers the wound with a sterile dressing. Terminology Burr hole: Hole drilled into the skull using a burr drill, also called trepanation or trephination. Debridement: The removal of an organ's dead, damaged, or infected tissue to facilitate natural healing of the remaining healthy tissue. Hemostasis: The stoppage of blood flow. Surgical mesh: Medical device used to repair or take the place of a tissue deficiency, and to provide additional support for weak or damaged tissue. Read Less

short_description: Craniotomy for repair of dural/cerebrospinal fluid leak, including surgery for rhinorrhea/otorrhea Notes: (For repair of spinal dural/CSF leak, see 63707, 63709)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider incises the skull and opens the cranium to repair a leak of cerebrospinal fluid, or CSF, which occurs as a result of a break in the dura, the outer membrane covering the brain. The dural repair also resolves drainage of CSF through the nose or the ear. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider verifies the location of the fracture and dural tear using a radiologic imaging technique such as magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI. The provider incises the scalp over the damaged area and retracts the scalp. Next, he removes a section of the skull, called a bone flap, to access the brain underneath by making one or more burr holes with a surgical drill. He then inserts a special surgical saw, called a craniotome, through the burr holes and creates a bone flap. The provider lifts and removes the bone flap to expose the dura, the outer protective covering of the brain. He then closes the damaged dura with sutures and may apply a synthetic graft or tissue sealant, such as fibrin glue, over the dural suture line to help close the tear and create a watertight seal. After the repair is complete, the provider replaces the bone flap, stabilizing and fixating it in place with tiny plates, wires, and screws as necessary. He inserts a temporary drain at the surgical site to prevent fluid buildup. Finally, he folds the tissue flap back, sutures the layers of scalp tissue together, and then covers the wound with a sterile dressing. short_description: Repair of encephalocele, skull vault, including cranioplasty
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider repairs the part of the brain that extends through a defect, or gap, in the cranial vault, the bones of the cranium enclosing the brain, and corrects the defect or deformity of the skull. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a scalp incision to expose the area around the cerebral herniation. The provider then separates the protruding cerebral tissue from the scalp tissue as necessary, taking care to minimize blood loss. Next, he removes a section of the skull, called a bone flap, to access the brain underneath by making one or more burr holes with a surgical drill. He then inserts a special surgical saw, called a craniotome, through the burr holes and creates a bone flap to access the encephalocele. He then carefully removes any nonfunctional cerebral tissue and returns the brain tissue and any membranes or fluids that have come out of the gap in the skull back into the skull. He removes the sac that surrounded the encephalocele and closes the damaged dura with sutures. He may apply a synthetic graft or tissue sealant, such as fibrin glue, over the dural suture line to help close the tear and create a watertight seal. Next, he replaces the bone flap and closes the skull using tiny plates, wires, and screws as necessary. Finally, he folds the tissue flap back, sutures the layers of scalp tissue together, and then covers the wound with a sterile dressing. short_description: Cranioplasty with autograft (includes obtaining bone grafts); up to 5 cm diameter
lay_term: The provider repairs a skull bone defect no larger than 5 cm by using bone tissue harvested from another part of the patient and transferred to the cranium. This service resolves cranial defects as a result of depressed skull fractures, congenital abnormalities, tumors, or other trauma or disease. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider places a skull fixation device, which is a head clamp that holds the patient’s head in position during the procedure. He may also place a lumbar drain in the lower back to help remove cerebrospinal fluid, or CSF, to allow the brain to relax during the procedure. Next, he makes an incision in the scalp over the skull defect, lifts the skin and muscles off the bone, and folds it back. He locates the defect and incises the cranium. Next, he uses the existing skull bone and bone grafts that he harvests from another location such as the cranial bone in uninvolved areas of the skull, the ribs, ilium, or other location to repair the defect. If the provider uses a cranium graft, for example, he may use a technique known as a split graft. In this harvesting procedure, he resects an uninvolved area of the skull in the same shape as the cranial defect, splits the outer and inner compact layers apart, and uses the outer layer to cover the defect and the inner layer to cover the donor site. He fixes them in place using miniplates, screws and wires. Finally, he folds the tissue flap back, sutures the layers of scalp tissue together, and then covers the wound with a sterile dressing. This procedure is done for a defect no larger than 5 cm in diameter. Terminology Autograft: Any tissue from one part of the body moved to another location on the same patient; also known as an autologous graft. Cranioplasty: A surgery to repair defects of the cranium. Cranium: Bones of the head. Ilium: Uppermost part of the hip bone. Tips Report 62146 for a defect of 5 cm or less, and report 62147 for a defect more than 5 cm. Read Less

short_description: Neuroendoscopy, intracranial; with dissection of adhesions, fenestration of septum pellucidum or intraventricular cysts (including placement, replacement, or removal of ventricular catheter)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider uses a small endoscope to access the brain to remove adhesions or a cyst located on the septum pellucidum or a cyst within one of the ventricles. The provider also places, replaces, or removes a ventricular catheter used for a shunt system or for external drainage. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a small incision in the scalp over the ventricular system where the cyst is located and then creates a small burr hole in the skull. He introduces a trocar through the burr hole and into the ventricular system, removes the stylet, the sharp, pointed, needle like inner part, and passes a neuroendoscope through the trocar into the hollow fluid filled compartment of the brain. The neuroendoscope provides illumination and magnification to identify the anatomy of the ventricular system and to locate the cyst. Using microsurgical techniques and direct visualization through the neuroendoscope, the provider inserts a small cutting catheter through the scope and perforates the front and back wall of the cyst, opening them to drain the cystic fluid into the chambers of the brain, which will absorb it. He continues to inspect the ventricular system, removing cyst adhesions and checking cerebrospinal fluid flow, or CSF, throughout the system. He may need to place, replace, or remove a ventricular catheter. He may also fenestrate the cyst using a laser inserted through the endoscope. To place a catheter, he backs the scope to a position away from the choroid plexus and advances the tip of the trocar to the same level as the neuroendoscope. He then removes the scope and places a ventricular catheter at the same location as the trocar to reduce the chance of obstruction. He may take a sample of CSF and send it to the lab for testing. He removes the trocar, and he connects the ventricular catheter to a shunt system or to a sterile external collection bag. Finally, he sutures the tissue scalp layers together and covers the wound with a sterile dressing. short_description: Ventriculocisternostomy, third ventricle
lay_term: The provider performs a ventriculocisternostomy, creating an artificial opening in the floor of the third ventricle of the brain to the cisterna magna, one of three principal openings in the subarachnoid space where cerebrospinal fluid, or CSF, drains. The provider performs this procedure to treat hydrocephalus, most often a form known as noncommunicating hydrocephalus to allow CSF to drain inside the patient’s body. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the front of the scalp. He then retracts the scalp exposing the skull. Next, he removes a section of the skull, called a bone flap, by making one or more burr holes with a surgical drill and creating the flap. The provider lifts and removes the bone flap to expose the dura. He opens the dura and incises down to the cortex below. Then he creates a tract to gain access to the lateral ventricle. Once inside the ventricular compartment, he identifies and enters the foramen of Monro and then enters the third ventricle. Here, he carefully punctures the floor of the ventricle and opens it, being cautious not to injure the critical vascular structures nearby. He moves through the opening into the cisternal space to ensure the patency of the opening, meaning that it is open and unobstructed and that CSF is freely flowing. short_description: Percutaneous lysis of epidural adhesions using solution injection (eg, hypertonic saline, enzyme) or mechanical means (eg, catheter) including radiologic localization (includes contrast when administered), multiple adhesiolysis sessions; 2 or more days Notes: (62263 includes code 77003)
lay_term: The provider places a catheter or introduces a chemical substance to an adhesion in the epidural space to remove the adhesion, in a procedure often referred to as a Racz catheter procedure or epidural neurolysis. The provider uses imaging to identify the site of the adhesions and the procedure occurs over more than one session and more than one day. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider, using fluoroscopy, introduces a needle into the epidural space at the appropriate vertebral level. He then passes a flexible catheter through the needle and into the space. He carefully moves the catheter around the space until he arrives at the target where the scar tissue is affecting the nerve root. Then he injects contrast to confirm the needle tip and catheter location. He also uses the contrast to determine the flow of liquid in the space, determine the amount of scarring, to evaluate the nerve roots and spinal nerves in the area, and to evaluate any constriction or swelling of the nerve. He decides on the substance and amount to inject then administers the chemical to the adhesion to dissolve the scar tissue and reduce the inflammation and irritation on the nerve. Or he manipulates the catheter to mechanically break up the adhesions. Then he dresses the wound. The provider repeats the procedure as necessary at 12 to 24 hours and again at 24 to 48 hours later. At each series of injections, he performs a repeat epidural contrast injection with fluoroscopic views to verify correct catheter placement and evaluate the surrounding epidural space. When he visualizes the gradual opening of constricted scar areas around the target nerves or nerve roots, the injections are complete, and he removes the catheter, and then applies a sterile dressing. Contrast: A special dye used in radiology imaging to improve the visibility of internal structures or organs of the body, which providers administer to patients through various routes, including oral and intravenously; also called contrast material, contrast medium, contrast media, contrast agent, or contrast dye. Epidural space: The space that surrounds the dura which is the outermost layer that surrounds the spinal canal; the epidural space houses the spinal nerve roots, blood and lymphatic vessels, and fatty tissues. Fluoroscopy: Fluoroscopy is a live X–ray where the X–ray image appears on a fluorescent screen television monitor; providers often use fluoroscopy to view body structures while performing procedures. Hypertonic saline: A sterile solution that contains sodium chloride, or salt. Lysis: The destruction of a cell by rupture of the cell wall membrane or breakdown by a chemical substance.
