short_description: Percutaneous aspiration within the nucleus pulposus, intervertebral disc, or paravertebral tissue for diagnostic purposes Notes: (For imaging, use 77003) (Do not report 62267 in conjunction with 10005, 10006, 10007, 10008, 10009, 10010, 10011, 10012, 20225, 62287, 62290, 62291)
lay_term: The provider aspirates fluid or tissue from the soft pads between the vertebrae of the spinal column, called the intervertebral discs. Or he aspirates fluid from within the paravertebral tissue (the tissue adjacent to the spinal column). He may also aspirate the gel–like substance in the middle of a spinal disc (nucleus pulposus). This diagnostic service helps to identify causes of disc inflammation such as bacterial or fungal infections. Explanation In this procedure, the provider positions the patient on his side or lying face down and after prepping and draping the patient, administers a local anesthetic at the proposed puncture site. Using fluoroscopy or computed tomography (CT) imaging guidance, the provider then introduces a hollow needle into the spinal column at the puncture site. She then advances the needle until she positions it in the disc or in the surrounding tissue. Then she verifies the needle placement using CT or fluoroscopic imaging. She then uses the needle to aspirate fluid and or cells, moving the needle and taking samples as necessary. She sends samples to the laboratory for diagnostic testing. Finally, she withdraws the needle and applies a sterile dressing. Terminology Computed tomography: Computed tomography (CT) is when the provider rotates an X–ray tube and X–ray detectors around a patient, which produces a tomogram, a computer generated cross sectional image; providers use CT to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases. Fluoroscopy: Fluoroscopy is a live X–ray where the X–ray image appears on a fluorescent screen television monitor; providers often use fluoroscopy to view body structures while performing procedures. Nucleus pulposus: Gel–like substance in the middle of a spinal disc. Paravertebral: Situated beside the vertebral column. Percutaneous: Through the skin. short_description: Spinal puncture, lumbar, diagnostic
lay_term: In this diagnostic procedure, the provider obtains a sample of the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) for examination. The provider commonly performs this procedure to rule out meningitis. Explanation When the patient is prepped and anesthetized, the provider identifies the space between the second and third or third and fourth lumbar vertebrae and marks it using a surgical marker. The provider inserts a spinal needle, taking care to avoid any injury to the nearby blood vessels. He advances the needle until CSF starts to leak out of it. The provider collects approximately 8 to 15 mL of CSF and sends it to pathology for further analysis. The provider then flushes the site with sterile saline and applies gauze at the site of needle insertion. Sometimes, if the procedure fails, the provider performs the procedure again under fluoroscopic guidance; this happens most commonly in obese patients. Terminology Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF): A clear watery fluid that originates and flows in the ventricles and all over the brain and spinal cord and helps to maintain consistent pressure in the brain and spinal cord. Fluoroscopic guidance: Use of fluoroscopy, a live X–ray where the image appears on a monitor, to view body structures while performing procedures. Lumbar spine: Lower back, containing vertebrae enumerated L1 through L5. Meningitis: Inflammatory disease of the meninges, the covering of the brain that occurs commonly due to bacterial or viral infections. mL: Abbreviation for milliliter, a metric unit of measure of volume; 1 mL equals approximately 0.034 U.S. fluid ounces; previously known as a cubic centimeter (cc). Spinal puncture: Extracting fluid from the spinal cord using a hollow needle for diagnostic purposes. Ventricles: Communication channels in the brain that is responsible for the production of the cerebrospinal fluid, CSF; there are four ventricles, third ventricle, fourth ventricle, and two lateral ventricles. Vertebra: One of the interlocking bones of the spine. Tips Providers most commonly perform this procedure either at the L2 to L3 level or L3 to L4 level of the lumbar spine. Code 62270 for diagnostic lumbar puncture and code 62272 for therapeutic spinal puncture do not include imaging guidance. If the provider uses imaging guidance, do not report these codes with an imaging guidance code. Instead, see 62328 for diagnostic lumbar spinal puncture with fluoroscopic or CT guidance and 62329 for therapeutic spinal puncture for drainage of cerebrospinal fluid by needle or catheter with fluoroscopic or CT guidance. lay_term: The provider obtains a sample of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) under fluoroscopic or CT imaging guidance and sends the specimen to the laboratory for examination. The provider commonly performs this procedure to rule out meningitis or help diagnose cerebral palsy. Explanation The provider positions the patient on his or her side with knees pulled up to the chest, or sitting, leaning forward on a stable surface. After prepping and draping the patient, the provider administers a local anesthetic at the proposed puncture site, first infiltrating the skin and then deeper tissue. The provider identifies the space between the second and third or third and fourth lumbar vertebrae and marks it using a surgical marker. The provider inserts a spinal needle under fluoroscopic or CT imaging guidance, taking care to avoid any injury to the nearby blood vessels. He advances the needle until CSF starts to leak out of it. The provider collects approximately 8 to 15 mL of CSF and sends it to pathology for further analysis. The provider then flushes the site with sterile saline and applies gauze at the site of needle insertion. Fluoroscopic guidance: Use of fluoroscopy, a live X–ray where the image appears on a monitor, to view body structures while performing procedures. Lumbar spine: Lower back, containing vertebrae enumerated L1 through L5. Meningitis: Inflammatory disease of the meninges, the three protective membranes covering the brain, that occurs commonly due to bacterial or viral infections. mL: Abbreviation for milliliter, a metric unit of measure of volume; 1 mL equals approximately 0.034 U.S. fluid ounces; previously known as cubic centimeter (cc). short_description: Spinal puncture, therapeutic, for drainage of cerebrospinal fluid (by needle or catheter)
lay_term: During this procedure, the provider reduces cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) pressure on the brain. He inserts a hollow needle or catheter into the subarachnoid space, usually in the lower back of the spinal column, to withdraw CSF. This procedure is also referred to as a spinal tap. Explanation In this procedure, the provider positions the patient on his or her side with knees pulled up to the chest, or sitting, leaning forward on a stable surface. After prepping and draping the patient, the provider administers a local anesthetic at the proposed puncture site, first infiltrating the skin and then deeper tissue. This area usually corresponds with the fourth and fifth lumbar space. She then inserts a needle between the two vertebrae, through the dura, and into the fluid–filled spinal canal. When fluid returns through the needle, the provider may attach a manometer, a special tube that attaches to the needle to measure the pressure of the CSF. The provider then may withdraw the fluid through the needle, or she may insert a catheter to siphon CSF, or she may allow it to drip out of the needle on its own and collect a small amount, about one tablespoon, in test tubes. In any case, she collects the fluid and sends it to the laboratory for testing. Finally, she withdraws the needle and applies a sterile dressing. After the procedure, the provider may have the patient continue to lie flat to reduce the incidence of a headache by not elevating his head or prevent leakage of fluid. Terminology Catheter: A flexible or rigid hollow tube placed into the body for administration of medication or fluids, to remove fluid or to keep a passage open. Dura: Outermost of the three layers that surround the brain and spinal cord. Lumbar vertebrae: Vertebrae situated between the thoracic, or chest, level vertebrae and the sacral, or bottom vertebrae, in the spinal column, indicated by the symbols L1 through L5. Subarachnoid space: The space between the arachnoid membrane and pia mater, the middle and innermost of the three membranes covering the brain. lay_term: The provider inserts a hollow needle or catheter into the subarachnoid space, usually in the lower back (lumbar spine) under fluoroscopic or CT imaging guidance and withdraws CSF to relieve pressure on the brain. This procedure is also referred to as a spinal tap. Explanation The provider positions the patient on his or her side with knees pulled up to the chest, or sitting, leaning forward on a stable surface. After prepping and draping the patient, the provider administers a local anesthetic at the proposed puncture site, first infiltrating the skin and then deeper tissue. This area usually corresponds with the fourth and fifth lumbar space. She then inserts a needle between the two vertebrae, through the dura, and into the fluid–filled spinal canal under fluoroscopic or CT imaging guidance. When fluid returns through the needle, the provider may attach a manometer, a special tube that attaches to the needle to measure the pressure of the CSF. The provider then withdraws CSF through the needle or she may insert a catheter to syphon CSF until the manometer indicates a more normal pressure. She collects a small amount, about one tablespoon, of CSF in a test tube and sends it to the laboratory for testing. Finally, she withdraws the needle and applies a sterile dressing. After the procedure, the provider may have the patient continue to lie flat for some time to reduce the incidence of a headache and prevent leakage of CSF. Terminology Cerebral palsy: Group of nonprogressive disorders of movement and posture caused by damage to the brain before birth or during the first few years of life and characterized by paralysis, lack of coordination and balance, and muscle spasms. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF): A clear watery fluid that originates and flows in the ventricles and all over the brain and spinal cord and helps to maintain a consistent pressure in the brain and spinal cord. Computed tomography (CT): An imaging procedure in which an X–ray tube and X–ray detectors rotate around a patient and produce a tomogram, a computer–generated three–dimensional image of the inside of an object from a large series of two–dimensional X–ray images taken around a single axis of rotation; providers use CT to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases. Fluoroscopic guidance: Use of fluoroscopy, a live X–ray where the image appears on a monitor, to view body structures while performing procedures. Lumbar spine: Lower back, containing vertebrae enumerated L1 through L5. Meningitis: Inflammatory disease of the meninges, the three protective membranes covering the brain, that occurs commonly due to bacterial or viral infections. mL: Abbreviation for milliliter, a metric unit of measure of volume; 1 mL equals approximately 0.034 U.S. fluid ounces; previously known as cubic centimeter (cc). Spinal puncture: Extracting fluid from the spinal cord using a hollow needle for diagnostic purposes. Vertebra: One of the interlocking bones of the spine. lay_term: The provider injects a patient's own blood to seal a cerebrospinal fluid, or CSF, leak that a spinal needle often causes. This service treats a post spinal headache which may occur when an epidural, spinal needle, or lumbar puncture leaves a hole or tear in the dura, the lining around the spinal cord, causing spinal fluid to leak. Explanation In this procedure, an anesthesia provider typically administers a blood patch to seal a spinal fluid leak. The provider positions the patient on his or her side with knees pulled up to the chest, or sitting, leaning forward on a stable surface. The provider cleans the area with an antiseptic solution and numbs it with a local anesthetic. Next, he inserts a needle into the patient’s arm and withdraws a small amount of blood. Then the provider injects the blood into the epidural space at the level of the leak in the same space or right next to the area where he injected the anesthetic to clot and seal the hole in the dura. He does this in a procedure similar to the original spinal injection or epidural that caused the leak. Then he withdraws the needle and applies a sterile dressing. He has the patient lay flat for a period of time and then slowly raises the patient’s head to a sitting position. Terminology Epidural block: Injection of a local anesthetic just outside the dura, the outermost of the three layers that surround the brain and spinal cord. Read Less

short_description: Injection/infusion of neurolytic substance (eg, alcohol, phenol, iced saline solutions), with or without other therapeutic substance; subarachnoid
lay_term: The provider injects or infuses a neurolytic, a substance that is used to kill a specific nerve or group of nerves, in the subarachnoid space of any spinal level. The provider may include another therapeutic drug along with the neurolytic. This service helps to eliminate severe pain, especially from cancer pain involving the torso. Explanation In this procedure, an anesthesia provider typically positions the patient on his or her side with knees pulled up to the chest and the affected side down. The provider cleans the target injection site with an antiseptic solution and numbs it with a local anesthetic. Next, the provider uses fluoroscopic guidance to insert the needle through the skin over the target location. She advances the needle slowly over short distances with intermittent fluoroscopic monitoring to determine the needle tip position. When she confirms satisfactory needle position, she may inject contrast to further determine the exact needle location. Once the provider reaches the subarachnoid level, she injects the neurolytic solution in increments, with time between injections to allow her to determine the effects and side effects of each increment, or she places a catheter to infuse the substance. The catheter also helps the provider by reducing complications that may occur with subarachnoid injections. She may use contrast to monitor the spread of the neurolytic. When the procedure is complete, she withdraws the needle but may leave the catheter in for future use and applies a sterile dressing. Terminology Catheter: A flexible or rigid hollow tube placed into the body for administration of medication or fluids, to remove a fluid or to keep a passage open. Contrast: A special dye used in radiology imaging to improve the visibility of internal structures or organs of the body, which providers administer to patients through various routes, including oral and intravenously; also called contrast material, contrast medium, contrast media, contrast agent, or contrast dye. Fluoroscopy: Fluoroscopy is a live X–ray where the X–ray image appears on a fluorescent screen television monitor; providers often use fluoroscopy to view body structures while performing procedures. Neurolytic: A neurodestructive agent. Subarachnoid space: The space between the arachnoid membrane and pia mater, the middle and innermost of the three membranes covering the brain. Tips This code includes contrast for the localization of contrast flow in the spine during and or after an injection, known as an epidurography. For nonneurolytic substances a provider administers via an injection or infusion into the subarachnoid or epidural space, see codes 62320 to 62327. Read Less

short_description: Injection/infusion of neurolytic substance (eg, alcohol, phenol, iced saline solutions), with or without other therapeutic substance; epidural, cervical or thoracic
lay_term: The provider injects or infuses a neurolytic, a substance that is used to kill a specific nerve or group of nerves, in the epidural space of the cervical or thoracic spinal level. The provider may include another therapeutic drug along with the neurolytic. This service helps to eliminate severe pain after trauma or surgery involving limb amputation or to manage acutely painful conditions such as cancer. Explanation In this procedure, an anesthesia provider typically positions the patient on his or her side with knees pulled up to the chest and the affected side down. The provider cleans the target injection site with an antiseptic solution and numbs it with a local anesthetic. Next, the provider uses fluoroscopic guidance to insert the needle through the skin over the target location. She advances the needle in a slow and deliberate manner. When she confirms a satisfactory needle position, she may inject contrast to further determine the exact needle location, and or she may gently aspirate to assure that the needle is not improperly positioned in the subarachnoid space, or it is not intravascular. If she aspirates cerebrospinal fluid, or CSF, the provider repeats the attempt at a different interspace. If she aspirates blood, she rotates the needle and repeats the aspiration test. Once the provider reaches the epidural space of the cervical or thoracic level, she slowly injects the neurolytic solution, or she places a catheter to infuse the substance. The catheter also helps the provider by reducing the risk of complications associated with epidural injections. She may use contrast to monitor the spread of the neurolytic. When the procedure is complete, she withdraws the needle and applies a sterile dressing. In some cases, the provider may repeat this procedure on a daily basis or every other day to treat acute painful disorders. Terminology Catheter: A flexible or rigid hollow tube placed into the body for administration of medication or fluids, to remove a fluid or to keep a passage open. Cervical vertebrae: Seven vertebra located in the upper neck of the spinal column, the vertebral column, indicated by the symbols C1 through C7. Contrast: A special dye used in radiology imaging to improve the visibility of internal structures or organs of the body, which providers administer to patients through various routes, including oral and intravenously; also called contrast material, contrast medium, contrast media, contrast agent, or contrast dye. Epidural space: The space that surrounds the dura which is the outermost layer that surrounds the spinal canal; the epidural space houses the spinal nerve roots, blood and lymphatic vessels, and fatty tissues. Interspace: Space between two body parts as in the space between two vertebral bodies, which contain the intervertebral disc; also called the intervertebral space. Intravascular: Within a vessel or vessels. Thoracic vertebra: Twelve vertebrae located between the cervical, or neck vertebrae and the lumbar, the lower back vertebrae, indicated by the symbols T1 through T12. Vertebrae: The bony segments that form the spine. There are 33 segments designated into 5 different levels: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral and 4 coccygeal. lay_term: The provider removes a small amount of the gel like substance in the middle of a spinal disc, known as nucleus pulposus. He makes a needle puncture through the skin and into the disc. Then he aspirates a small amount of disc material between two vertebrae in the lumbar region of the spine to relieve pressure on the nerves of the spine. The provider uses fluoroscopy or other imaging technique for visualization. The procedure may include epidural anesthetic injections to one or more treatment levels of the lumbar region. Explanation In this procedure the provider uses one of several methods to decompress or remove disc material from a disc that is protruding through two or more vertebrae in the lumbar portion of the spine. In any method, the provider uses fluoroscopy, and injects contrast into the gel like center, or nucleus, of the suspect spinal disc, in a procedure known as a discography. This is done to better visualize the disc and protruding material. The provider also uses fluoroscopy guidance, along with a local epidural anesthetic injection, when necessary, to perform a lumbar decompression. To begin, the provider places the patient on a radiolucent table and the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized. The provider inserts a needle through a stab wound in the flank, or side of the patient and guides the needle into the disc interspace, being careful not to puncture the dura. After puncturing the disc, he confirms the proper positioning of the needle using the fluoroscopic images. Next, he either manually, or using an automated device, radiofrequency, or laser energy, aspirates disc tissue, removing as much material as he safely can until he decompresses the nerve. Terminology Disc or Intervertebral disc: This is a round, flat fibrous tissue layer between two adjacent vertebrae that consists of a hard outer layer called annulus fibrosis and a gel like central part called nucleus pulposus; The intervertebral disc acts as a flexible cushion between the two vertebrae that helps in load bearing and shock absorption. Dura: Outermost of the three layers that surround the brain and spinal cord. Epidural injection: Anesthetic injection administered to the nerve roots in the epidural space, the space that surrounds the dura, for analgesic or pain relief. Fluoroscopy: Fluoroscopy is a live X–ray where the X–ray image appears on a fluorescent screen television monitor; providers often use fluoroscopy to view body structures while performing procedures. Lumbar vertebrae: Five vertebrae situated between the thoracic, or chest, level vertebrae and the sacral, or bottom vertebrae, in the spinal column, indicated by the symbols L1 through L5. Radiolucent: Transparent to X–rays. Tips Do not separately report fluoroscopic guidance because imaging is included in code 62287 as the descriptor indicates. Imaging is required during and after the insertion of a needle into the disc interspace to allow the provider to see during aspiration and removal of the disc tissue from the space. Read Less

short_description: Injection procedure for discography, each level; lumbar
lay_term: The provider performs this diagnostic procedure, called discography, by injecting contrast into the nucleus pulposus, or gel like center of a spinal disc, to examine and better visualize the intervertebral disc space. This procedure is also referred to as a discogram, or disc stimulation, and it helps identify damage to lumbar vertebrae causing neck or back pain. Explanation In this procedure, the provider uses contrast and imaging to evaluate the discs of the lumbar spine. The provider begins by positioning the patient on a radiolucent table, with the patient resting on one side and rolled slightly forward on the table. The provider cleans the skin over the area for injection with an antiseptic, typically the lowest two or three lumbar disc levels, and then injects a local anesthetic to numb the skin and soft tissue overlying each disc. Using fluoroscopic guidance, she carefully guides a needle through the skin and muscle and comes to rest on the outer layer of the disc. She passes a second needle through the first needle and inserts it into the center of the suspect intervertebral disc, then injects contrast through the needle and into the nucleus, or center, of the disc. The provider takes images and evaluates the disc anatomy and dye pattern, looking for leaks outside of the disc. She also assesses the patient’s response during and after each injection to determine if the pain is concordant, meaning similar to what the patient has been feeling, different, or if the patient feels no pain at all. She repeats this process for each level necessary. When the procedure is complete, she places a sterile dressing over the wound. short_description: Injection procedure for chemonucleolysis, including discography, intervertebral disc, single or multiple levels, lumbar
lay_term: The provider performs this procedure, called chemonucleolysis, by injecting an enzyme into a lumbar vertebral disc to dissolve the bulging nucleus pulposus, or the gel like center of the spinal disc. The provider also performs a discography using fluoroscopy to locate the disc and determine the exact area where the injection should be given. This procedure treats a herniated disc and relieves back pain as a result of bulging disc material that is putting pressure on the spinal nerve. Explanation In this procedure, the provider injects chymopapain, an enzyme from the papaya fruit, to speed up the breakdown of the gel like substance inside a protruding lumbar disc. As a result, the bulging disc may shrink and relieve pressure on the spinal nerve. The provider begins by positioning the patient on one side and rolled slightly forward on a radiolucent table. She cleans the skin over the area for injection with an antiseptic and then injects a local anesthetic to numb the skin and soft tissue overlying one or more lumbar levels. Using fluoroscopic guidance, she carefully guides a needle through the skin and muscle and into the center of the suspect intervertebral disc. She uses the needle, or may insert another through the first, and she injects saline or water to verify correct needle placement in the nucleus, or center, of the disc. In the same manner, she injects contrast to ensure that the disc is only bulging and not ruptured. If the disc is bulging and has not broken open, the provider continues with the procedure. Next, the provider usually injects a small test dose of the enzyme and waits a short period of time to ensure the patient is not allergic to the substance. She will then inject the full dose of chymopapain and after a few minutes remove the needle. She repeats this process for each level necessary. When the procedure is complete, she applies a sterile dressing. Terminology Disc or Intervertebral disc: A round, flat, fibrous tissue layer between two adjacent vertebrae that consists of a hard outer layer, called annulus fibrosis, and a gel like central part, called nucleus pulposus; the intervertebral disc acts as a flexible cushion between the two vertebrae that helps with load bearing and shock absorption. Fluoroscopy: Fluoroscopy is a live X–ray where the X–ray image appears on a fluorescent screen television monitor; providers often use fluoroscopy to view body structures while performing procedures. Lumbar vertebrae: Five vertebrae situated between the thoracic, or chest level vertebrae and the sacral, or bottom vertebrae, in the spinal column, indicated by the symbols L1 through L5. Radiolucent: Transparent to X–rays. Vertebrae: The bony segments that form the spine. There are 33 segments designated into 5 different levels: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral and 4 coccygeal. Tips Report radiographic imaging and saline acceptance testing separately. short_description: Myelography via lumbar injection, including radiological supervision and interpretation; cervical Notes: (Do not report 62302 in conjunction with 62284, 62303, 62304, 62305, 72240, 72255, 72265, 72270)
lay_term: The provider administers an injection of contrast into the lumbar area of the spine and performs myelography at the cervical region. The provider also performs radiological supervision and interpretation of the procedure. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider initiates the procedure by injecting contrast in the subarachnoid space in the lumbar region of the spine. The subarachnoid space is an area where cerebrospinal fluid circulates between the arachnoid and pia mater, which are membranes surrounding the brain and spinal cord. The contrast spreads along the length of the spinal cord, and the provider uses imaging, typically fluoroscopy, to view and examine the spinal cord, nerve roots, and other structures in the cervical region. The provider documents an interpretation of the imaging service. Terminology Cervical spine: Neck, containing vertebrae enumerated C1 through C7. Fluoroscopy: Fluoroscopy is a live X–ray where the X–ray image appears on a fluorescent screen television monitor; providers often use fluoroscopy to view body structures while performing procedures. Injection: Use of a syringe to forcibly instill a liquid substance into tissues, vessels, or tumors; the instilling of a medicinal substance using various routes that include subcutaneous, below the skin, intravenous, within a vein, or intramuscular, into a muscle, among others; also, excessive accumulation of blood in an area causing redness. Lumbar spine: Lower back, containing vertebrae enumerated L1 through L5. Myelography: Imaging procedure in which the provider injects a contrast medium into the subarachnoid space to view and examine the spinal structures. Nerve root: Portion of a nerve where it connects to the central nervous system; origin of a nerve. Spinal cord: Group of nerve fibers encased in the vertebral column that connects the brain to the rest of the body. Tips Codes 62302 to 62305 all describe myelography via lumbar injection along with radiological supervision and interpretation. Your code choice varies on the myelography region or regions: 62302, cervical; 62303, thoracic; 62304, lumbosacral; 62305, two or more regions. When the provider does not perform both the injection and radiological services, the injecting provider should report the appropriate injection code, such as 62284, Injection procedure for myelography and/or computed tomography, lumbar. The radiological provider should report the appropriate code from the range 77240 to 77270. Read Less

short_description: Injection(s), of diagnostic or therapeutic substance(s) (eg, anesthetic, antispasmodic, opioid, steroid, other solution), not including neurolytic substances, including needle or catheter placement, interlaminar epidural or subarachnoid, cervical or thoracic; without imaging guidance
lay_term: The provider injects a diagnostic or a therapeutic substance, such as pain medication or a steroid, into the space around the spinal nerves of the cervical (neck) or thoracic (upper and middle back) region. She inserts a needle or catheter (tube) to facilitate the injection but does not use imaging guidance. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and the area anesthetized, the provider advances a needle into the skin, toward the interlaminar epidural or subarachnoid space in the cervical or thoracic region. She confirms the location of the needle, taking care to avoid any injury to nearby nerve roots or the spinal cord. The provider then injects a substance, such as an epidural steroid solution, for either diagnostic or therapeutic purposes, and monitors the patient for 15 to 20 minutes after the injection. Interlaminar: Refers to the space between the laminae of the vertebrae, bony structures at the back of each vertebra that form the spinal canal. Nerve root: The portion of a nerve where it connects to the central nervous system; the origin of a nerve. Neurolytic: Refers to anything that destroys a nerve. Opioid: Substance that is used to relieve pain; morphine being the most common opiate. Steroid: Chemical substances that include drugs for reducing pain, inflammation, and swelling, like prednisone. Subarachnoid space: Space between the arachnoid and pia mater, membranes covering the brain and spinal cord through which the cerebrospinal fluid flows. short_description: Implantation, revision or repositioning of tunneled intrathecal or epidural catheter, for long-term medication administration via an external pump or implantable reservoir/infusion pump; without laminectomy
lay_term: The provider implants, replaces, or repositions a previously implanted and tunneled intrathecal or epidural catheter. This procedure does not include a laminectomy. This service is done to instill medication into the cerebrospinal fluid using an external or internal reservoir pump system to treat many conditions including severe pain after trauma, postoperative pain, pain from diseases like cancer, or for other medical conditions such as spasticity, a muscle control disorder in which muscles are tight or stiff, and they involuntarily spasm. Explanation In this procedure, the provider implants a catheter or he replaces or adjusts a previously placed catheter in the spinal cord. The catheter that he inserts or adjusts is subcutaneously tunneled and connected to an implantable or external pump for long term medication administration. If the provider is implanting the pump, once the patient is appropriately positioned, prepped and draped, the provider uses fluoroscopy to identify the proper location. He introduces a catheter into the proper level, either the epidural space outside the dura, or carefully continuing through into the intrathecal space within the spinal fluid. The provider verifies the catheter placement and patency, meaning that it is open and unobstructed. Next, he exposes the strong, fibrous cord that runs through the spine called the supraspinous ligament and sutures the catheter to it. He may insert an anchoring sleeve also suturing it in place in the tissue, and then place the catheter into the sleeve to prevent tension or movement of the catheter. The provider then tunnels the catheter to the site where he implants an internal reservoir or pump or where one already resides. He may also connect the catheter to an external unit. When the procedure is complete, he closes and dresses the wound. Terminology Catheter: A flexible or rigid hollow tube placed into the body for administration of medication or fluids, to remove a fluid, or to keep a passage open. Dura: Outermost of the three layers that surround the brain and spinal cord. Epidural catheter: Catheter residing in the area outside and surrounding the dura mater of the spinal cord. Epidural space: The space that surrounds the dura which is the outermost layer that surrounds the spinal canal; the epidural space houses the spinal nerve roots, blood and lymphatic vessels, and fatty tissues. Intrathecal catheter: Catheter residing inside the spinal cord in the cerebral spinal fluid. Lamina: The posterior arch of a vertebra, or the back part of the vertebra, that covers the spinal canal. Laminectomy: Removal of a portion of the vertebra called the lamina, which is the posterior arch or the back part of the vertebra that covers the spinal canal. Tips This procedure includes epidural or intrathecal catheter revision, such as repositioning or replacing the catheter. You should separately report the implantation of the subcutaneous reservoir or pump. Medicare assigns codes 62350 and 62351 a global period of 10 days. Read Less

short_description: Removal of previously implanted intrathecal or epidural catheter
lay_term: The provider removes a previously implanted and tunneled intrathecal catheter, which may be necessary due to infection or the patient no longer requiring medication administration. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider identifies the prior surgical site to access the reservoir pump. He then reopens the incision over the implanted device and releases the sutures that anchor the catheter in place. He disconnects the catheter from the pump and removes the catheter, withdrawing it from its location in the spine. Next, he closes the catheter track to reduce cerebrospinal fluid leakage or possibility of infection. The provider may also remove the implanted reservoir. short_description: Implantation or replacement of device for intrathecal or epidural drug infusion; subcutaneous reservoir
lay_term: The provider implants or replaces a reservoir under the skin for intrathecal or epidural infusion of medications, such as anesthetics, antispasmodics, opioids, steroids, and other solutions to treat pain and administer chemotherapy. Explanation In this procedure, the provider places a drug reservoir subcutaneously for the infusion of medications through a tunneled catheter into the intrathecal or epidural space. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision at the placement site, typically in the abdomen. If the procedure is an initial implant, she creates a pocket in the deep subcutaneous tissue and places a reservoir into the pocket. Using a tunneling device, she makes a subcutaneous tunnel between the reservoir and the spinal incision, attaches a spinal catheter to the tunneling device with a suture, and she pulls the spinal catheter through the subcutaneous tunnel to the reservoir. Next, she verifies the catheter patency, meaning that it is open and unobstructed, and she connects the catheter to the reservoir and secures it with sutures. If she is replacing an existing reservoir, she reopens the scar from the placement procedure. She then removes the previously implanted reservoir, replaces it with a new one, and attaches the existing implanted catheter, suturing it to the reservoir to secure the connection. When the procedure is complete, she irrigates the wound, then closes and dresses the incision. Terminology Antispasmodic: A substance that relieves convulsions or spasms. lay_term: The provider removes all or some of a bulging intervertebral disc and/or removes bony portions of the surrounding vertebrae to decompress, or relieve pressure from, the spinal cord and nerve roots in a patient with back pain. She uses an endoscopic approach and performs the procedure at a single interspace level. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider injects contrast, a type of dye, into the jellylike center, or nucleus, of the suspect spinal disc, and visualizes the disc and any protruding material under imaging guidance. The provider introduces the endoscope through an endoscope sheath inserted over a guidewire, after needle localization. She then removes some or all of the disc material, a discectomy, either manually or with an automated device, radiofrequency ablation, or laser energy. Alternatively, or in addition, she excises the bony arches of the vertebrae (laminotomy) or some of the bony surface of the vertebrae that forms the spinal canal (foraminotomy). She may also perform a facetectomy, excising the facets, the small joints that form the articulating, or contacting, surfaces of the vertebrae. She ensures complete decompression of the spinal cord and nerve roots and then irrigates the surgical area, removes all instruments, and closes the incisions. Terminology Endoscopy: Examination of a hollow organ or cavity using an instrument specially designed for the procedure. Intervertebral disc: A round, flat, fibrous tissue layer between two adjacent vertebrae, the interlocking bones of the spine, consisting of a tough outer layer called the anulus fibrosus and a jellylike central part called the nucleus pulposus, that acts as a flexible cushion between the vertebrae to aid in load bearing and shock absorption. Nerve root: The portion of a nerve where it connects to the central nervous system; the origin of a nerve. Radiofrequency ablation, or RFA: Use of heat produced by focused radio waves, a type of electromagnetic wave, to destroy areas of abnormal, damaged, or diseased tissue. Vertebrae: The bony segments that form the spine; there are 33 segments divided into five different levels. Tips Do not separately report fluoroscopic guidance because imaging is included in this code. Imaging is required during and after the insertion of an endoscope and needle to allow the provider to see during the procedure. Read Less

This procedure does not contain a facetectomy, foraminotomy, or discectomy. Explanation During a laminectomy, the surgeon removes the spinous process (the bony projection on the back of the vertebrae) and one or both lamina (the broad plates of bone on either side of the spinous process that complete the "arch" of the vertebrae and enclose the spinal cord), followed by decompression of the nerves. The focus of the work is the individual vertebra and the nerve roots emanating through the foramen (passageways) on either side of the vertebra. The surgeon may perform a laminectomy on several adjacent vertebral levels depending on the condition of the patient. Tips To report a laminectomy and hemilaminectomy (laminotomy) correctly, you must know whether the surgeon removed one or more complete laminae from a single vertebra or if they partially removed the laminae from two adjacent vertebrae. short_description: Transpedicular approach with decompression of spinal cord, equina and/or nerve root(s) (eg, herniated intervertebral disc), single segment; thoracic
lay_term: The provider uses a transpedicular approach to repair a bulging thoracic disc without manipulating the spinal cord. The approach is through the side of the pedicle of one thoracic vertebra. This service is done to relieve pressure on the spinal cord, equina, or nerve roots. Explanation In this procedure, the provider performs a procedure to relieve pressure from a bulging disc in the thoracic spine. The provider performs this service primarily for discs in which the bulge is lateral, or toward the left or right side of the spinal canal, where nerve roots branch off. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider locates the correct spinal level using fluoroscopy. He makes a lateral incision over the spine at the levels adjacent to the herniated disc, then dissects down through the tissue, retracts the soft tissues, and dissects the adjacent muscles. Using an operating microscope for visualization, he locates the pedicle adjacent to the herniated disc space. He exposes and removes the facet joint and lamina of the pedicle. Next, he incises the lateral disc space of the protruded disc, identifying the disc fragments from normal disc material. The disc fragments are calcified or firm, and the provider removes the disc fragments causing the spinal cord compression. When he achieves adequate decompression, he removes the retractors, reapproximates the layers, sutures the wound, and applies a sterile dressing. He may apply a local anesthetic to the incision to minimize postoperative incisional pain. Terminology Annulus fibrosus: Exterior of the intervertebral disc. Decompression: A procedure to remove pressure on a structure. Dura: Outermost of the three layers that surround the brain and spinal cord. Equina: The bundle of spinal nerve roots at the end of the spinal cord. Facet joint: A pair of joints present in the posterior aspect of the spine; they are common sources of neck and lower back pain; also known as the zygapophyseal joint. Fluoroscopy: Fluoroscopy is a live X–ray where the X–ray image appears on a fluorescent screen television monitor; providers often use fluoroscopy to view body structures while performing procedures. Herniated disc: Herniation occurs when an intervertebral disc moves out of its place, there is a tear in the annulus of the cervical disc from an accident or pathological causes, and the nucleus pulposus bulges out; a herniated disc puts pressure on the nerve roots or spinal cord and causes pain in the patient; when medication fails, herniation needs surgical intervention. Lamina: The posterior arch of a vertebra, or the back part of the vertebra that covers the spinal canal. Nucleus pulposus: The gel like substance in the middle of a spinal disc. Operating microscope: Binocular microscope, meaning two eyepieces, for simultaneous viewing with both eyes used to view fine structures during operations. Pedicle: A paired part of the vertebral arch, the posterior part of a vertebra that connects a lamina to the vertebral body. Segment: One of the thirty portions of the nerves of the spinal cord contained within the vertebral column; spinal cord segments do not correspond to vertebral segments. Thoracic spine: The twelve vertebrae located between the cervical, or neck vertebrae and the lumbar, the lower back vertebrae, indicated by the symbols T1 through T12. Vertebrae: The bony segments that form the spine. There are 33 segments designated into 5 different levels: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral and 4 coccygeal. Tips Report 63055 for a thoracic segment. Report 63056 for a lumbar segment. Report 63057 for each additional lumbar or thoracic segment. Read Less

lay_term: The provider uses a transpedicular approach to repair a bulging lumbar disc without manipulating the spinal cord. The approach is through the side of the pedicle of one lumbar vertebra, known as a transpedicular approach. A far lateral herniated intervertebral disc may require a different approach such as a transfacet or lateral extraforaminal approach. This service is done to relieve pressure on the spinal cord, equina, or nerve roots. Explanation In this procedure, the provider performs a procedure to relieve pressure from a bulging disc in the lumbar spine. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider locates the correct spinal level using fluoroscopy. He makes a midline incision over the herniated disc and dissects subcutaneous tissues to the side of the midline, then elevates and retracts the muscles. Using an operating microscope, the provider removes a piece from the side of the bone that joins the facet joints along with a portion of the lamina and facet joint to visualize the disc space. The provider then removes a portion of the lateral part of the protruded disc to decompress the nerve, identifying the disc fragments from normal disc material. The disc fragments are calcified or firm, and the provider removes the disc fragments causing the spinal cord compression. When he achieves adequate decompression, he applies an anesthetic to the nerve root for pain control. He removes the retractors, reapproximates the layers, sutures the wound, and applies a sterile dressing. The provider may use an alternate approach for far lateral herniated intervertebral discs, making a posterior incision and dissecting to allow for a more complete exposure of the spine. This approach allows the provider to remove posterior spinal structures, such as the lamina and facet joints, and expose the spinal nerve, dorsal root ganglion, and the disc prolapse. Far lateral disc herniation occurs most often at the L4/L5 and L3/L4 levels. Terminology Annulus fibrosus: Exterior of the intervertebral disc. Decompression: A procedure to remove pressure on a structure. Disc prolapse: To fall or slip out of place, as of an organ or part. Dorsal root ganglion: Cluster or group of sensory nerve cell bodies that are part of the posterior, or dorsal, root of each spinal segmental nerve. Equina: The bundle of spinal nerve roots at the end of the spinal cord. Facet complex: The two facet joints along with disc space create a three joint complex that allow flexion/extension, rotation, and lateral movement of the spine. Facet joint: A pair of joints present in the posterior aspect of the spine; they are common sources of neck and lower back pain; also known as the zygapophyseal joint. Fluoroscopy: Fluoroscopy is a live X–ray where the X–ray image appears on a fluorescent screen television monitor; providers often use fluoroscopy to view body structures while performing procedures. Herniated disc: Herniation occurs when an intervertebral disc moves out of its place, there is a tear in the annulus of the cervical disc from an accident or pathological causes, and the nucleus pulposus bulges out; a herniated disc puts pressure on the nerve roots or spinal cord and causes pain in the patient; when medication fails, herniation needs surgical intervention. Intertransverse muscles: The muscles between the bony protrusion on either side of the arch of a vertebra, known as the transverse process and the adjacent vertebrae. Lamina: The posterior arch of a vertebra, or the back part of the vertebra, that covers the spinal canal. Lateral extraforaminal approach: Surgical incision to the side of the midline in the area of the transverse processes, the small bony projections to the right and left side of each vertebra, and the facet joints; the provider then dissects through the intertransverse muscles and ligament to expose the lateral disc and exiting nerve root. Nucleus pulposus: The gel like substance in the middle of a spinal disc. Operating microscope: Binocular microscope, meaning two eyepieces, for simultaneous viewing with both eyes used to view fine structures during operations. lay_term: The provider excises (removes) part or all of a thoracic vertebra via a transthoracic (anterior chest) approach and decompresses the spinal cord and/or nerve roots at an additional level in the upper back after the first excision. Explanation The provider resects each additional thoracic vertebral segment using a transthoracic approach, which includes decompressing the spinal cord and or nerve root. Under anesthesia, the physician makes an incision and removes the diseased and damage part of the vertebral bone. This relieves pressure on the spinal cord. Then the physician removes the discs above and below the vertebrae and inserts bolts below and above the vertebrae. The physician opens the vertebral gap and inserts a bone graft. Once that is complete, the physician closes the vertebral gap and inserts a metal plate. Terminology Corpectomy: Surgical excision of the main body of a vertebra, one of the interlocking bones of the back. Nerve root: The portion of a nerve where it connects to the central nervous system, i.e., the brain or spinal cord; the origin of a nerve. Spinal cord: Group of nerve fibers encased in the vertebral column that connects the brain to the rest of the body. Vertebrae: The bony segments that form the spine and protect the spinal cord; there are 33 segments divided into five different levels — the neck (cervical spine, C1 through C7), upper and middle back (thoracic spine, T1 through T12), lower back (lumbar, L1 through L5), sacral (sacrum, S1 through S5), and tail bone (coccyx which consists of 4 fused bones). Tips There are many similarities among vertebral corpectomy, anterior discectomy, partial excision of vertebrae, and osteotomy of the spine which makes choosing among these codes a real challenge. If a difficult operative report overwhelms you, slow down and identify the component steps that distinguish the differences between each procedure. Your most effective tool to distinguish among spinal procedures is a firm grasp of what each code set includes: For example, an anterior vertebral corpectomy, also sometimes called a vertebral body resection, involves a total or near–total removal of the vertebral body. All vertebral corpectomy procedures include discectomy and can occur either with spinal canal decompression (CPT® codes 63081–63091) or with the excision of an intraspinal lesion (CPT® codes 63300–63308), the latter of which involves decompression of the spinal cord and/or nerve root(s). When reporting a vertebral corpectomy with decompression (CPT® codes 63081–63091), you should not report fracture care separately, even though it is common with procedures of this type. You may, however, separately bill for arthrodesis (CPT® codes 22548–22812, to stabilize the spine) and spinal reconstruction procedures, including bone grafts (CPT® codes 20930–20938) and spinal instrumentation (CPT® codes 22840–22855). Additional Info Example: To treat a compressed nerve caused by fracture, the surgeon performs discectomies followed by a corpectomy of segments C4 and C5. The physician frees compressed nerve roots and reconstructs the spine using a tricortical allograft and titanium plates. Although the surgeon removes only two vertebral bodies, the arthrodesis occurs across three interspaces. The instrumentation involves four segments because the fixation will extend above and below the two reconstructed segments. In this case, you would report CPT® codes: 63081, +63082, 22554, +22585 x 2, +20931, +22846 Read Less

short_description: Vertebral corpectomy (vertebral body resection), partial or complete, lateral extracavitary approach with decompression of spinal cord and/or nerve root(s) (eg, for tumor or retropulsed bone fragments); thoracic, single segment
lay_term: The provider removes part of or an entire thoracic vertebral bone and intervertebral disc material in a procedure called a corpectomy. In this procedure, a lateral extracavitary, or LECA, approach is made to one thoracic vertebra to relieve pressure on the spinal cord and spinal nerves. This approach also allows for the stabilization of the spine at the same time. The service is usually done as a result of a fracture, tumor, or deformity. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a midline incision near the thoracic tumor or fracture and curves the incision outward to the side, exposing the bundle of paraspinal muscles over the target location. The provider divides and elevates the muscles from the ribs and retracts them toward the midline. Using fluoroscopy, she identifies the correct vertebral segment, and she dissects the associated ribs from the muscles and underlying membrane that lines the lung and wall of the thoracic cavity. Next, she resects the ribs in one piece. Using a surgical drill, she removes the transverse processes, the small bony projections to the right and left side of each vertebra, and part of the facet and pedicle to expose the side of the dura and vertebral body. She expands the operative field further by gently retracting the nerve root and surrounding structures. Next, she uses the drill to remove the central part of the vertebral body exposing any bone fragments or tumors along the spinal cord or nerve roots. Using a curette, she removes the fragments or tumor and then uses the tool, along with a rongeurs, to remove the affected disc. She examines the area for dural tears and obtains hemostasis. If necessary, she fuses, reconstructs, and or grafts the intervertebral body to stabilize the spine by scraping cartilage and preparing the bone for fusion or reconstruction with harvested bone, or using graft material. When the procedure is complete, she places a drain in the space then closes the opening in layers and applies sterile dressings. Dura: Outermost of the three layers that surround the brain and spinal cord. Facet: Smooth area on a bone. Fluoroscopy: Fluoroscopy is a live X–ray where the X–ray image appears on a fluorescent screen television monitor; providers often use fluoroscopy to view body structures while performing procedures. Hemostasis: The stoppage of blood flow. Lateral extracavitary approach: A surgical approach to the spine, incising along the middle of the back and then turning sharply toward one side to follow the general direction of the ribs of the patient; the incision resembles an L and is often referred to as a hockey stick incision. Paraspinal muscles: The band of muscles that run next to the spine that support and move the spine. Pedicle: A paired part of the vertebral arch, the posterior part of a vertebra, that connects a lamina to the vertebral body. Rongeurs: A surgical instrument with a sharp, scoop shaped tip, used for removing small pieces of bone or tough tissue. Thoracic vertebra: Twelve vertebrae located between the cervical, or neck vertebrae and the lumbar, the lower back vertebrae, indicated by the symbols T1 through T12. Vertebrae: The bony segments that form the spine. There are 33 segments designated into 5 different levels: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral and 4 coccygeal. The provider excises the lamina. Laminae are the broad plates of bone on either side of the spinous process that complete the “arch” of the vertebrae and enclose the spinal cord. The provider identifies the spinothalamic tracts, which are sensory pathways to the thalamus, the area of the brain where sensory information converges. The provider divides the dentate ligament (triangular ligament that anchors the spinal cord to the dura mater, which is the thick membrane around the cord), dissects the tissue in front of the anterior spinal artery, and closes the incision in layers. lay_term: In this procedure, the provider releases a tethered spinal cord. A tethered spinal cord is a progressive congenital or trauma induced neurological disorder. Abnormal tissue attachments form around the spine, most often at the base, and limit the movement of the spinal cord within the spinal column. This procedure is done to correct functional abnormalities in the lower extremity, referred to as neurological deficits and to stabilize neurologic progression. Explanation The goal of this procedure is to untether the spinal cord from the surrounding adhesions and restore its location in the spinal canal. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized and face down, the provider makes an incision over the area in the lumbar spine where it is tethered. He then gains access to the spinal cord by dissecting and retracting the soft tissues and muscles off the spine. Next, he removes a portion of the lumbar vertebra, called the lamina, in a procedure known as a laminectomy. Using an operating microscope, he opens the dural tube, the fibrous sheath covering the spinal cord. He then releases the tissue attachments to the end of the spinal cord and separates the cord and nerve roots from the surrounding adhesions and thick fibrous band to untether the cord, taking care not to injure the nerves. If he identifies no additional abnormalities such as a cyst or tumor, he closes the dural tube, reconstructing it, and then closes the layers of the muscle, fascia, and skin, and applies sterile dressings. lay_term: In this procedure, the provider removes or closes off a tangle of arteries and veins that have abnormal communications between them. short_description: Vertebral corpectomy (vertebral body resection), partial or complete, for excision of intraspinal lesion, single segment; extradural, lumbar or sacral by transperitoneal or retroperitoneal approach
lay_term: The provider uses a transperitoneal (through the interior lining of the abdomen) or retroperitoneal (anterolateral) approach to perform a partial or complete excision of the main body of a single vertebra, one of the interlocking bones of the back, to remove an extradural lesion within the lumbar or sacral spine. Explanation The provider resects a single lumbar or sacral vertebral segment to remove an extradural lesion. Under anesthesia, the physician makes a transperitoneal or retroperitoneal incision and removes the diseased and damaged part of the vertebral bone. This relieves pressure on the spinal cord. Then the physician removes the discs above and below the vertebrae and inserts bolts below and above the vertebrae. The physician opens the vertebral gap and inserts a bone graft. Once that is complete, the provider closes the vertebral gap and inserts a metal plate. Terminology Corpectomy: Surgical excision of the main body of a vertebra, one of the interlocking bones of the back. Diskectomy, discectomy: Surgical removal of all or a part of an intervertebral disc. Extradural: Present inside the skull but outside the dura mater, which is the thick, outermost membrane covering the brain or within the spine but outside the dural sac enclosing the spinal cord, nerve roots and spinal fluid. Intervertebral disc: A round, flat, fibrous tissue layer between two adjacent vertebrae, the interlocking bones of the spine, consisting of a tough outer layer (anulus fibrosus) and a jellylike central part (nucleus pulposus) that acts as a flexible cushion between the vertebrae to aid in load bearing and shock absorption. Intradural: Within the dura, the tough outer membrane surrounding the central nervous system. Lesion: Area of damaged or diseased tissue, particularly an area that is well–defined. Lumbar spine: The lower back region containing vertebrae L1 through L5. Osteotomy: The cutting of bone for treatment purposes. Retroperitoneal incision: Incision behind and outside the peritoneum, the membrane covering the organs of the abdominal cavity; also referred to as an anterolateral incision. Sacrum: Large, triangular bone at the end of the vertebral column. Spinal cord: Group of nerve fibers encased in the vertebral column that connects the brain to the rest of the body. Transperitoneal incision: An incision that cuts through the peritoneum, the membrane that encloses the abdominal organs and lines the abdominal cavity. Tips CPT® codes 63300–63308 describe the removal of the vertebral body to gain access to an intraspinal lesion. Select these codes according to location (cervical, thoracic, or lumbar/sacral), approach (anterior/anterolateral, transthoracic, thoracolumbar, transperitoneal, or retroperitoneal) and whether the surgeon cuts into the dura (the fibrous membrane that forms the outer covering of the central nervous system). If the surgeon cuts into the dura, it is an "intradural" procedure; it not, it's extradural. As with CPT® codes 63081–63091, report the appropriate code for the first vertebra removed, using add–on CPT® code 63308 for each additional segment. As with CPT® codes 63081–63091, you may claim arthrodesis and spinal reconstruction separately. For example, if the surgeon uses an anterior approach to access segments C4 and C5, opening the dura and exposing the tumor for excision, report the primary procedure using CPT® codes 63304 and 63308. You may report any grafts and/or instrumentation for spinal reconstruction separately. There are many similarities among vertebral corpectomy, anterior discectomy, partial excision of vertebrae, and osteotomy of the spine which makes choosing among these codes a real challenge. If a difficult operative report overwhelms you, slow down and identify the component steps that distinguish the differences between each procedure. Read Less

The radiation oncologist reports the appropriate code(s) for clinical treatment planning, physics and dosimetry, treatment delivery and management from the Radiation Oncology section (77261-77790). short_description: Percutaneous implantation of neurostimulator electrode array, epidural
lay_term: Lay Term
guidelines: Surgery Guidelines Range Specific Guideline For electronic analysis with programming, when performed, of spinal cord neurostimulator pulse generator or transmitters, see codes 95970, 95971, 95972. Test stimulation to confirm correct target site placement of the electrode array(s) and/or to confirm the functional status of the system is inherent to placement, and is not separately reported as electronic analysis or programming of the neurostimulator pulse generator or receiver system. Electronic analysis (95970) at the time of implantation is not separately reported. Codes 63650, 63655, 63661, 63662, 63663, 63664 describe the operative placement, revision, replacement, or removal of the spinal neurostimulator system components to provide spinal electrical stimulation. A neurostimulator system includes an implanted pulse generator or implanted receiver with an external transmitter, a collection of contacts, electrodes (electrode array), an extension if applicable, an external controller, and an external charger, if applicable. The neurostimulator may be integrated with the electrode array (single-component implant, see 0784T, 0785T) or have a detachable connection to the electrode array (two or more component implant). Multiple contacts or electrodes (4 or more) provide the actual electrical stimulation in the epidural space. For percutaneously placed neurostimulator systems (63650, 63661, 63663), the contacts are on a catheter-like lead. An array defines the collection of contacts that are on one catheter. For systems placed via an open surgical exposure (63655, 63662, 63664), the contacts are on a plate or paddle-shaped surface. short_description: Laminectomy for implantation of neurostimulator electrodes, plate/paddle, epidural
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider removes a portion of the vertebra called the lamina and places a permanent plate/paddle electrode in the epidural space, or area between the dura membrane and the wall of the vertebra for spinal cord stimulation. This procedure is done when a larger area of coverage is necessary or to reduce the risk of movement of the electrode array. Providers perform this procedure to control pain and spasms. Explanation This procedure involves careful placement of permanent plate/paddle electrodes in the epidural space for spinal cord stimulation including the necessary work to anchor the electrodes to the interspinal ligaments, position and implant a pulse generator, tunnel and connect the paddle leads, and program the system for the special pattern of stimulation along with any necessary postoperative care. After a successful spinal cord stimulation trial, and once the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider uses fluoroscopy to see the existing percutaneous leads. He then incises the skin and tissue over that site on the spine, and using loupe magnification or an operating microscope dissects down through the tissue, fascia, and muscles to expose the spinous processes and lamina. He verifies the location again using fluoroscopy, and he removes the portion of the vertebra over the location of the percutaneous lead and removes the percutaneous leads. Continuing to use magnification, the provider then places the plate/paddle lead into the epidural space closest to the point to be treated. He uses fluoroscopy again to verify the exact placement of the leads, then tests them and anchors the plate or paddle to the fibrous tissue to prevent movement. Next, the provider passes the extension lead subcutaneously using a tunneling device from the back and around the patient’s side to the lower abdomen where he makes an incision to implant the neurostimulator or electronic pulse generator, which is a separately reportable procedure. He connects the lead or leads to the generator, then tests the leads to verify they are functioning properly. The provider secures the generator in the fibrous tissue under the skin and closes the incision. When the procedure is complete, he closes the spinal incision in layers and covers it with sterile dressings. The provider applies stimulation within days after the procedure. Terminology Dura: The outermost layer of membrane that surrounds the spinal canal. Electrode array: Device that contains multiple plates or electrodes. Epidural space: The space that surrounds the dura, which is the outermost layer of membrane that surrounds the spinal canal. The epidural space houses the spinal nerve roots, blood and lymphatic vessels, and fatty tissues . Electronic pulse generator or neurostimulator: A device that produces low voltage electrical pulses, with a regular or intermittent waveform, that creates a mild tingling or massaging sensation that stimulates the nerve pathways. Fluoroscopy: Fluoroscopy is a live X–ray where the X–ray image appears on a fluorescent screen television monitor; providers often use fluoroscopy to view body structures while performing procedures. Lamina: A part of a vertebral arch that covers the back surface of the spinal canal, forming a protective roof over the spinal cord. Loupe magnification: A magnifying eyepiece used to see small details more closely. Plate/paddle electrodes: An electrode array that consists of contacts positioned on a plate or paddle shaped surface. Spinous process: The bony ridges that projection off the back of each vertebra where the muscles and ligaments of the spine attach. Tips The implantation of the spinal neurostimulator pulse generator or receiver is a separately reportable procedure under code 63685, Insertion or replacement of spinal neurostimulator pulse generator or receiver, direct or inductive coupling. You may need to append modifier 58, Staged or related procedure or service by the same physician during the postoperative period, to 63655 and to 63685, if the provider performs these services during the postoperative period of the initial trial insertion. short_description: Revision including replacement, when performed, of spinal neurostimulator electrode percutaneous array(s), including fluoroscopy, when performed Notes: (Do not report 63663 in conjunction with 63661, 63662 for the same spinal level)
lay_term: The provider revises and or replaces a previous placed permanent percutaneous electrode array for spinal cord stimulation. This service includes fluoroscopy when necessary. short_description: Repair of meningocele; less than 5 cm diameter
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider repairs a birth defect called a meningocele in which the meninges, the membranous coverings of the brain and spinal cord, protrude through a defect in the skull or spinal column forming a sac filled with cerebrospinal fluid. The diameter of the meningocele is less than 5 cm. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision immediately adjacent to the bulging meningeal sac. He then carries the incision down and into the sac in an area free of neural structures. He then retracts the skin edges and mobilizes the nerve roots that course back into the spinal canal. He sacrifices the nerve roots that terminate in the sac. He then pushes the protruding neural tissues back into the spinal canal and restores the normal structure of the spinal cord. He then locates the filum terminale connective tissue and cuts it sharply to release the associated connection of the spinal cord. He then dissects the dura membrane from the connective tissue. He then performs watertight closure of the dural defect and reinforces the closure by suturing in the midline the paravertebral muscles and fascia. He next sutures the skin in layers and covers the wound with a sterile dressing. The diameter of the meningocele is less than 5 cm. Terminology Dura: Outermost of the three layers that surround the brain and spinal cord. Filum terminale: A strand of connective tissue that extends from top to bottom providing vertical support to the spinal cord. Tips Code 63700 does not include complex skin repair. Read Less

short_description: Repair of myelomeningocele; less than 5 cm diameter
lay_term: The provider repairs a birth defect called a myelomeningocele, a severe form of spina bifida, in which the spinal membrane and spinal cord protrude through a defect in the vertebral column. The diameter of the myelomeningocele is less than 5cm. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision immediately adjacent to the myelomeningocele, which commonly occurs in the lumbar or sacral areas of the lower back. She then carries the incision down and into the sac in an area free of neural structures. She then retracts the skin edges and mobilizes the nerve roots that course back into the spinal canal. She excises the nerve roots that terminate in the sac as necessary. She then sutures the edges of the neural folds to form and restore the normal structure of the spinal cord. The provider then locates the point at which the spinal cord terminates, known as the filum terminale, and she cuts the connective tissue sharply to release the associated connection of the spinal cord. She then dissects the dura membrane from the connective tissue. Next, she performs a watertight closure of the dural defect and reinforces the closure by suturing in the paravertebral muscles and tissue. The provider may place small subcutaneous drains along the patient’s flank, or sides. Finally, she sutures the skin in layers and covers the wound with a sterile dressing. The goal of this procedure is to prevent infection and damage to the spinal cord. The provider may use magnification during the procedure, and the diameter of the myelomeningocele in this procedure is less than 5 cm. Terminology Dura: Outermost of the three layers that surround the brain and spinal cord. short_description: Repair of myelomeningocele; larger than 5 cm diameter Notes: (Do not use modifier 63 in conjunction with 63704, 63706) (For complex skin closure, see Integumentary System)
lay_term: The provider repairs a birth defect called a myelomeningocele, a severe form of spina bifida, in which the spinal membrane and spinal cord protrude through a defect in the vertebral column. The diameter of the myelomeningocele is larger than 5cm. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision immediately adjacent to the myelomeningocele which commonly occurs in the lumbar or sacral areas of the lower back. She then carries the incision down and into the sac in an area free of neural structures. She then retracts the skin edges and mobilizes the nerve roots that course back into the spinal canal. She excises the nerve roots that terminate in the sac as necessary. She then sutures the edges of the neural folds to form and restore the normal structure of the spinal cord. The provider then locates the point at which the spinal cord terminates, known as the filum terminale, and she cuts the connective tissue sharply to release the associated connection of the spinal cord. She then dissects the dura membrane from the connective tissue. Next, she performs a watertight closure of the dural defect and reinforces the closure by suturing in the paravertebral muscles and tissue. The provider may place small subcutaneous drains along the patient’s flank, or sides. Finally, she sutures the skin in layers and covers the wound with a sterile dressing. The goal of this procedure is to prevent infection and damage to the spinal cord. The provider may use magnification during the procedure and the diameter of the myelomeningocele in this procedure is larger than 5 cm. Terminology Dura: Outermost of the three layers that surround the brain and spinal cord. Filum terminale: A strand of connective tissue that extends from top to bottom providing vertical support to the spinal cord. short_description: Repair of dural/cerebrospinal fluid leak, not requiring laminectomy
lay_term: The provider repairs a tear in the dura that causes a cerebrospinal fluid, or CSF, leak and can lead to a serious infection. The dura is the tough outer membrane surrounding the central nervous system. This service may be necessary to repair a defect that occurs after spinal or intradural surgery, trauma, or a congenital abnormality. Explanation After the provider obtains careful imaging studies to locate the dural breach, and the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider uses careful surgical technique and magnification to incise the skin over the site of the dural tear and dissects down to the tear. She retracts the soft tissues and adjacent muscles then explores the site to locate and repair any cause of the tear such as a sharp piece of bone, which she removes. She suctions CSF from the incision. If she finds no breach in the dura, she closes the tear with a watertight primary closure by tightly reapproximating the wound edges to each other and suturing. If it is a large defect or a thin dura that cannot hold sutures, the provider prepares a tissue graft of dura, muscle, or fat or a synthetic dural substitute to close the wound without compression and create the watertight seal. If the tear is in a surgically inaccessible location, the provider may place the graft into the defect and tack the graft down to the margins inside the dural opening to prevent displacement of the graft. When the provider ensures a watertight seal and the procedure is complete, she closes the incision in layers and covers it with sterile dressings. Terminology Cerebrospinal fluid: The protective body fluid present in the dura, the membrane covering the brain and spinal cord . Laminectomy: Removal of a portion of the cervical vertebra called the lamina, which is the posterior arch or the back part of the vertebra that covers the spinal canal, in order to decompress the spinal cord and/or spinal nerve root. short_description: Creation of shunt, lumbar, subarachnoid-peritoneal, -pleural, or other; including laminectomy
lay_term: The provider implants a shunt, which is a small tube the provider places in the lumbar region near the base of the spine to drain cerebrospinal fluid, or CSF, from the cavity surrounding the spinal cord, known as the subarachnoid space. The procedure reduces pressure and diverts an overabundance of CSF to the abdominal, or peritoneal, cavity. The procedure may also divert CSF to the pleural or thoracic, cavity or to another area. The procedure includes a laminectomy where the provider removes a portion of the vertebra to access the surgical site. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the selected lumbar vertebrae and removes a portion of the vertebra called the lamina, which is the posterior arch of a vertebra, or the back part of the vertebra that covers the spinal canal. She then accesses the spinal cord by retracting the soft tissues and adjacent muscles. She inserts the shunt, a small catheter, into the dura, the outer covering of the spinal cord, and into subarachnoid space. Then she confirms CSF flow. She tunnels the catheter under the skin, around the patient’s side, over the hip bone or rib cage, to the abdominal or chest cavity, where the organs will absorb the CSF and pass it out through the body. She may use a purse string suture, a continuous, circular, inverting suture around the catheter, to reduce the risk of the catheter moving. When the procedure is complete, she closes the incision in layers and covers it with sterile dressings. Terminology Cerebrospinal fluid or CSF: The protective body fluid present in the dura, the membrane covering the brain and spinal cord . Lumbar vertebrae: Vertebrae situated between the thoracic, or chest, level vertebrae and the sacral, or bottom vertebrae, in the spinal column, indicated by the symbols L1 through L5. Tips Report code 63740 when the provider performs a laminectomy for shunt placement. Report code 63741 when the provider places the shunt without excising the lamina. Read Less

short_description: Posterior tibial neurostimulation, percutaneous needle electrode, single treatment, includes programming Notes: (Do not report 64566 in conjunction with 64555, 95970-95972) (For peripheral nerve transcutaneous magnetic stimulation, see 0766T, 0767T)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider applies electrical stimulation to the posterior tibial nerve by inserting a needle electrode through the skin. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider inserts the needle electrode in the ankle near the tibial nerve. He places a surface electrode over the medial aspect, meaning near the middle, of the calcaneus, or heel bone, on the same leg. He then connects the needle electrode to an external pulse generator. He then turns on the generator that delivers the pulse to the tibial nerve. The posterior tibial nerve arises from lumbosacral nerves L4–S3, which control the bladder muscles and perineal floor. The goal of this procedure is to treat overactive bladder, OAB, and the associated symptoms of urinary urgency, urinary frequency, and urge incontinence. Terminology Perineal floor: Also called the pelvic floor; comprised of a group of muscles that supports the pelvic organs and assists in urinary and fecal continence.
