short_description: Open implantation of cranial nerve (eg, vagus nerve) neurostimulator electrode array and pulse generator Notes: (Do not report 64568 in conjunction with 61885, 61886, 64570) (For open implantation of vagus nerve integrated neurostimulation system, see 0908T, 0909T)
lay_term: The provider uses an open approach to implant a cranial nerve neurostimulator electrode array and also implants a programmable pulse generator. The provider may perform this service to treat seizures, depression, and other disorders. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision to access the target cranial nerve, such as incising the side of the neck to expose the vagus nerve. The provider inserts an electrode array (multiple contacts) around the nerve. The provider makes another incision, often in the chest or arm, to create a pocket for the pulse generator. The provider passes a lead (wire) subcutaneously (under the skin) using a tunneling device. The tunnel goes from the area where the electrodes are to the generator pocket. Once the lead is in proper position, the provider carefully attaches and secures the electrodes to the nerve in its proper position and then attaches the lead to the generator pack. A neurostimulator works by the small, electronic pulse generator stimulating the electrodes around the nerve. The provider tests the unit. Once tests are successful, the provider secures the pack into the pocket. The provider then closes the wounds. Terminology Lead: An insulated wire connected to a pulse generator that sends electrical impulses through the wire to an electrode at the other end; providers may refer to leads as wires or electrodes or make reference to an electrode at the end of a lead. Pulse generator: Electronic device that stimulates the nerves that control muscles with electrical impulses. Vagus nerve: Cranial nerve X, one of the twelve nerves of the brain that emerge from the lower portion of the brain (cranial nerves); it is the longest cranial nerve and is involved in sensory and motor function of the respiratory and digestive system as well as the heart. Tips See 64582–64584 for hypoglossal nerve stimulator array services. Read Less

short_description: Revision or replacement of cranial nerve (eg, vagus nerve) neurostimulator electrode array, including connection to existing pulse generator Notes: (Do not report 64569 in conjunction with 64570 or 61888) (For replacement of pulse generator, use 61885)
lay_term: The provider replaces or revises a vagus nerve electrode array and its connections to an existing pulse generator. This service is generally done for an electrode array or pulse generator component malfunction or infection the patient develops from the implanted device. Explanation A neurostimulator electrode replacement or revision includes location of the electrode array around the left vagus nerve within the carotid sheath and replacing or revising the array, including reattachment to the existing electronic pulse generator pack. In this procedure, after the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision through the scar from the original operation over the vagus neurostimulator electrode array, and she disconnects the lead from the generator. Next, she incises the scar over the electrodes and carefully traces the lead to the anchored electrode array. Using loupe magnification or an operating microscope, the provider uses microsurgical techniques to expose the electrodes, and she gently dissects them from the nerve. She may adjust the electrodes or if the provider is replacing the electrode array, she exposes the vagus nerve further to place new electrodes at a new position on the nerve. She then attaches a new array, tunnels the new lead subcutaneously to the subclavicular pocket, attaches the lead to the existing generator pack, and tests the unit. Once tests are successful, she secures the pack into the pocket. The provider then closes the wounds and skin with sutures and or tissue adhesive. Terminology Carotid artery sheath: Protective sheath of fibrous tissue surrounding the carotid artery, one of the two main arteries or passageway carrying blood from the heart to other parts of the body, located on both sides of the neck, that supply blood to the brain. Cranial nerve or vagus nerve: One of the twelve nerves of the brain that emerge from the lower portion of the brain and supply various tissues of the head and neck. Electrode array: Device that contains multiple plates or electrodes. Electronic pulse generator: A device that produces low voltage electrical pulses with a regular or intermittent waveform that creates a mild tingling or massaging sensation that stimulates the nerve pathways. Loupe magnification: A magnifying eyepiece used to see small details more closely. lay_term: The provider removes a vagus nerve electrode array and existing pulse generator. Report this service only when the provider removes both the electrode array and the pulse generator without replacing them. This service may be done due to infection or the patient is unresponsive or intolerant to treatment. Explanation A neurostimulator electrode removal includes location of the electrode array around the left vagus nerve within the carotid sheath and removing the array, including the lead and existing electronic pulse generator pack. Using loupe magnification or an operating microscope, the provider uses microsurgical techniques to expose the electrodes, and she gently dissects them from the nerve. short_description: Open implantation of neurostimulator electrode array; neuromuscular
lay_term: The provider uses an open approach to implant a neuromuscular neurostimulator electrode array. This service is done for various reasons, such as to prevent or slow muscle atrophy or to relax muscle spasms through treatment of a motor nerve, or to decrease pain by treatment of a sensory nerve. The provider then closes the wound. Terminology Pulse generator: Electronic device that stimulates the nerves that control muscles with electrical impulses. Read Less

short_description: Open implantation of neurostimulator electrode array; sacral nerve (transforaminal placement)
lay_term: The provider uses an open approach to implant a sacral nerve neurostimulator electrode array. Placement is transforaminal, meaning through the foramen (the opening sacral nerves run through). short_description: Open implantation of hypoglossal nerve neurostimulator array, pulse generator, and distal respiratory sensor electrode or electrode array
lay_term: The provider uses an open approach to implant a hypoglossal nerve neurostimulator electrode array and also implants a programmable pulse generator and one or more distal respiratory sensor electrodes. The hypoglossal nerve innervates the tongue, and the provider may perform this service to treat sleep apnea, in which breathing stops intermittently during sleep. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision to access the hypoglossal nerve, which innervates the tongue. The provider inserts an electrode array (multiple contacts) around the nerve. The provider makes another incision, often in the chest, to create a pocket for the pulse generator. The provider passes a lead (wire) subcutaneously (under the skin) using a tunneling device. The tunnel goes from the area where the electrodes are near the jaw to the generator pocket. The provider also places a respiration sensing electrode or electrode array, typically lower in the chest. A respiration sensing lead attaches the implanted distal respiratory sensor to the implanted pulse generator. The provider secures the electrodes to the nerve and ensures the leads are attached to the pulse generator. The system uses the respiration sensor electrode or electrode array to monitor breathing. During each breath, the pulse generator delivers a signal to the electrode array at the hypoglossal nerve. The nerve activates muscles of the upper airway to keep the airway open during sleep, which may help patients with sleep apnea. The provider tests the unit. Once tests are successful, the provider secures the pack into the pocket. The provider then closes the wounds. Terminology Lead: An insulated wire connected to a pulse generator that sends electrical impulses through the wire to an electrode at the other end; providers may refer to leads as wires or electrodes or make reference to an electrode at the end of a lead. Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA): A condition occurring during sleep in which breathing stops intermittently for brief periods, disrupting the sleep cycle and resulting in daytime sleepiness; it is caused by obstruction, narrowing, or incompetence of the airway. Pulse generator: Electronic device that stimulates the nerves that control muscles with electrical impulses. Read Less

short_description: Revision or removal of peripheral neurostimulator electrode array
lay_term: The provider revises or removes a neurostimulator electrode array on a peripheral nerve, the portion of the nervous system lying outside the brain and spinal cord. This service is generally done for a neurostimulator component malfunction or because the patient develops an infection related to neurostimulator placement. Explanation A peripherally implanted neurostimulator, or nerve stimulator, transmits electrical impulses to nerves outside of the brain and spinal cord. It involves implanting electrodes around a selected peripheral motor or sensory nerve. The electrodes or leads then attach to a subcutaneously placed receiver or electronic pulse generator unit, which stimulates the nerve. Sciatic and ulnar nerves are often the sites of such an implantation. In this procedure, the provider revises or removes a peripherally implanted electrode array. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision through the scar from the original operation over the peripheral neurostimulator electrodes, and she carefully traces the leads to their anchored electrodes. Using loupe magnification or an operating microscope, the provider uses microsurgical techniques to expose the electrodes. She may adjust the electrodes for a revision, or she may remove the electrode array by gently dissecting them from the nerve. The provider then closes the wounds and skin with sutures and or tissue adhesive. Terminology Electrode array: Device that contains multiple plates or electrodes. Electronic pulse generator: A device that produces low voltage electrical pulses with a regular or intermittent waveform that creates a mild tingling or massaging sensation that stimulates the nerve pathways. Loupe magnification: A magnifying eyepiece used to see small details more closely. Peripheral motor nerve: Portion of the nervous system lying outside the brain and spinal cord that carries messages from the brain and spinal cord to the muscles to stimulate muscle contraction and make the body move. Sciatic nerve: One of the seven major peripheral nerves; innervates the skin and muscles of the posterior thigh, leg, and foot. Sensory nerve: A nerve that passes messages between different parts of the body and the brain or spinal cord to signal pain, pressure, and other sensations. Ulnar nerve: One of the seven major peripheral nerves; innervates the skin and muscles of the medial arm, forearm, and hand, plus the little finger and ring finger. Tips If the patient is still in a 90–day global period from the initial insertion, you may need to append modifier 78, Return to the operating room for a related procedure during the postoperative period, to 64585. For removal of the associated electronic pulse generator use 64595, Revision or removal of peripheral or gastric neurostimulator pulse generator or receiver. If the electrodes and generator are both removed, you can report both 64585 and 64595. You only use these two codes if your provider removes, but does not replace, the lead or generator. For replacement of the electrode, you’ll just report 64585. This coding includes the incisional placement of a new electrode. Read Less

lay_term: The provider inserts or replaces a peripheral, sacral, or gastric neurostimulator pulse generator or receiver. The system is one that requires surgical creation of a pocket for placement and that requires a connection between the electrode array and the pulse generator or receiver. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the skin at the location of the peripheral, sacral, or gastric neurostimulator pulse generator or receiver implantation site. Gastric nerves are a network of nerves that control the function of the stomach. The provider creates a pocket, or, if replacing an already implanted device, dissects the old device from the pocket and disconnects the lead(s) to the electrode array. If replacing the generator or receiver, the provider attaches the separately implanted lead(s) to the new generator. For an initial implant, the provider subcutaneously passes the lead(s) from the electrode array by using a tunneling device to the implanted neurostimulator pulse generator or receiver, and connects the lead(s) to the generator or receiver. The provider may perform test stimulations to confirm the system is working. The provider secures the generator or receiver in the pocket and closes the incision. short_description: Neuroplasty; digital, 1 or both, same digit
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider uses an open approach to incise scar tissue or other sources of pressure to relieve tension on one or both digital nerves in a single finger or toe. Digital nerves are sensory nerves that run along each side of a finger or toe along with arteries and innervate the fingers and thumb. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision into the target site in the patient’s finger where the compressed nerve is present. He then locates the compressed nerve and performs external neurolysis, releasing the nerve by cutting down the surrounding scar and soft tissues without entering into the nerve. He may also remove any bone spur or damaged muscle putting pressure on the nerve. He closes the incision in layers once he has repaired and freed the nerve. Terminology Bone spur: Bony projection that occurs along a joint; also called an osteophyte. External neurolysis: Removing the surrounding scarring from a nerve without entering into the nerve. Neuroplasty: Surgery to repair a nerve. Tips Use 64702 for open neuroplasty. It includes external neurolysis. Use add–on code 64727 for internal neurolysis done with an operating microscope. short_description: Decompression; unspecified nerve(s) (specify)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs a decompression of an unspecified nerve, freeing it from surrounding ligaments, which are exerting pressure on the nerve. The provider specifies the nerve decompressed in his documentation. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision into the target site where the compressed nerve is present. He further deepens the incision below the subcutaneous tissues. He exposes the ligament where the nerve is compressed due to overgrowth or shrinking of surrounding ligament tissue enclosing the nerve. With a sharp instrument, he dissects the ligament tissue and creates space for the nerve. After confirming decompression of the nerve, he closes the skin and subcutaneous layer with sutures. Once the service is complete, the provider documents in the patient’s medical record the specific nerve decompressed and the reason or reasons why the procedure was performed. Neurolysis: Application of heat, cold, or chemicals to a nerve to temporarily destroy the nerve. Tips When billing the payer for this service, include the provider’s documentation that shows the actual nerve decompressed and the patient’s condition. short_description: Suture of digital nerve, hand or foot; 1 nerve

Explanation The provider accesses the digital nerve through an open wound, or he makes an incision in the skin and through the subcutaneous tissue, carefully dissecting down to expose the nerve. He carries out the dissection using high power magnification and takes care not to injure the surrounding structures. He then sutures the healthy nerve ends together without creating tension. If the damaged nerve has motor as well as sensory functions, he gathers a group of nerve fibers and sutures them together. He then closes the wound or incision. Terminology Digital nerve: Any of the branches of nerves that supply the fingers, thumb, and toes. Motor nerve: A nerve that carries messages from the brain and spinal cord to the muscles to stimulate muscle contraction and make the body move. Sensory nerve: A nerve that passes messages between different parts of the body and the brain or spinal cord to signal pain, pressure, and other sensations. As the code descriptor indicates, you report +64832 for each additional digital nerve the provider sutures. For example, if the provider sutures two digital nerves of the hand and one digital nerve of the foot, then report 64831 for the first digital nerve sutured and report +64832 twice, once for the second digital nerve of the hand and again for the suture of the digital nerve of the foot. short_description: Suture of facial nerve; infratemporal, with or without grafting
lay_term: The provider repairs and may graft the facial nerve located in the temple. The procedure restores sensory and/or motor functions when the nerve becomes damaged or severed as a result of trauma or a facial nerve tumor. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider accesses the injured facial nerve through the open wound or by incising the temple area. She identifies the nerve involved, then gently and carefully mobilizes the nerve ends leaving as much of the nerve in its bed as possible so as not to disturb the blood supply. She trims the nerve to expose the healthy tissue using high–power magnification and taking great care to ensure the size of the two nerve ends align closely. She sutures the healthy nerve ends together without creating tension. If she can’t rejoin the nerve segment due to tumor resection or excessive nerve damage that creates a large gap between the nerve ends, then she grafts the nerve to repair it. To do this, she uses a cable graft, or inter–positional graft, often done with the sural nerve from the back of the calf or with the great auricular nerve found on the side of the neck. To obtain the nerve graft she incises the location over the donor nerve. She then identifies and frees a segment of the donor nerve. She removes the length needed and places it on moist gauze. She then repairs the donor nerve by joining the transected nerve ends and suturing them together. Then she closes the donor site incision. She then takes the donor nerve graft and sutures it to the ends of the transected nerve taking care to surround the donor nerve with enough soft tissue to protect it from external trauma. She also checks to make sure there is no obstruction or compression of the graft to ensure innervation is not impaired. Then she closes the wound or incision. Terminology Infratemporal: Below the temple. Cable or inter–positional nerve graft: A substitute, similar diameter, multi–strand replacement nerve used to replace a damaged or severed nerve. Tips For repair of an extracranial facial nerve see 64864. Read Less

short_description: Anastomosis; facial-spinal accessory
lay_term: The provider makes a surgical connection between the facial nerve and the spinal accessory nerve, which do not naturally connect. This procedure restores facial motor function after facial nerve loss from a tumor or injury that causes paralysis. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider accesses the facial and spinal accessory nerves by incising the side of the neck. She then isolates and confirms the spinal accessory nerve by stimulating the nerve. She then carefully trims back the outermost layer of the spinal accessory nerve using high–power magnification and takes care not to injure the jugular vein and other surrounding structures. She does the same for the facial nerve, exposing the fine nerve filaments of both nerves, but she tries not to divide the facial nerve, allowing it to remain in place to help with nerve repair. She sutures the spinal accessory nerve to the facial nerve without creating tension, and closes the wound or incision. Terminology Anastomosis: Surgical connection or joining of vessels or organs that don’t normally connect. Facial nerve: The seventh paired cranial nerve that supplies motor functions to facial muscles and sensory functions to the tongue. Facial–spinal accessory: Pertaining to the facial nerve and spinal accessory nerve. Spinal accessory nerve: The eleventh paired cranial nerve that provides motor function to control the two muscles of the neck used in head movement. Read Less

short_description: Nerve graft (includes obtaining graft), head or neck; up to 4 cm in length
lay_term: The provider uses a healthy nerve segment up to 4cm long to replace a damaged portion of a nerve in the head or neck. The procedure restores sensory and/or motor functions when the nerves become damaged or severed as a result of injury or trauma. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider harvests a nerve graft, usually from the sural nerve, a sensory nerve in the leg, by incising just behind the ankle bone and extending the incision upward as needed. She then identifies and frees a segment of the sural nerve up to 4cm in length. She removes the segment needed and places it on moist gauze. She then repairs the donor nerve by joining the sural nerve ends and suturing them together. Then she closes the leg incision. Next she incises the location over the damaged nerve and resects and removes the damaged portion of the nerve. She then takes the donor nerve graft and sutures it to the ends of the transected nerve taking care to surround the donor nerve with enough soft tissue to protect it from external trauma. She also checks to make sure there is no obstruction or compression of the graft to ensure innervation is not impaired. Then she closes the wound. Terminology Innervation: To supply the organs and other body parts with nerves. Nerve graft: Replacing a portion of a damaged nerve with a segment of a healthy nerve. Tips The term nerve graft in the common portion of the descriptor, i.e., the part left of the semicolon for 64885 and 64886, is singular, indicating that each code represents a single nerve graft. Therefore, if the provider grafts more than one nerve during a single operative session, report 64885 or 64886, as appropriate, for the first nerve graft. short_description: Nerve pedicle transfer; first stage
lay_term: The provider transfers a portion of a less important, healthy, donor nerve to a damaged recipient nerve to help the nerve tissue reconnect faster and recover its function faster. Explanation In this first stage procedure, the provider reroutes or transfers a portion of an intact healthy nerve from a donor nerve to a damaged nerve. On reaching the orbital apex, or peak, he clamps the tissues, makes an incision, and extracts the contents. He places dry gauze in the orbit, closes the wound using sutures, and applies a pressure patch. Terminology Exenteration: Removal of the eye and orbital soft tissues which may or may not include the eyelids, extraocular muscles, orbital fat, and optic nerve; also removal of other internal organs. lay_term: The provider repairs a tear wound in the cornea and or sclera, then repositions or removes some of the vascular middle layer of the eye due to a trauma to the globe. Explanation In this procedure, the physician repairs a corneal and or scleral laceration with correction of uveal tissue. The cornea is the transparent membrane of the outer layer of eyeball. The sclera is the white of the eye. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider begins by locating and inspecting the laceration site. Then she dries the corneal surface and trims any unhealthy tissue around the laceration site. If the provider finds protruding uveal tissue, she repositions it using a soft sweeping technique through a separate incision at the border of the cornea. The physician then uses fine sutures, and repairs the laceration to bring the edges of the wound together. If necessary, the provider next addresses the scleral laceration by gently incising conjunctival tissue around the cornea as necessary to expose the wound. The provider then excises any lost vitreous, the clear, jelly like substance through which light passes, and she repositions the uvea using an ocular spatula or similar instrument as necessary. The provider then sutures the scleral wound and dissects the protruding tissue incrementally after placing each suture. When the repair is complete, the provider administers subconjunctival antibiotic injections and applies an eye pressure patch. lay_term: The provider inserts an intraocular lens prosthesis after extracapsular cataract extraction using complex techniques and devices. He may perform this by means of an iris expansion device, providing support to the intraocular lens, or capsulorrhexis. This procedure is done without the use of an endoscopic laser probe to shrink the ciliary processes, a procedure to treat glaucoma. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, typically by application of local anesthesia to the eye, the provider makes a small incision in the eye and then enters the capsule and removes the hard nucleus from the lens of the eye. He may use an iris expansion device to aid in achieving stable dilation of the pupil. He then evacuates the soft lens cortex, leaving the capsule partially intact. He uses a microscope to assist with visualization. Finally, he inserts a prosthetic intraocular lens after irrigation and aspiration (I&A). The provider may also use phacoemulsification, where he uses an ultrasonic device to break up the cloudy lens and then uses I&A to remove it from the eye. He then inserts the intraocular lens prosthesis. The provider may also provide support to an intraocular lens by suturing it behind the iris if the capsule support is not sufficient to hold the lens. The provider might also employ primary posterior capsulorrhexis to remove posterior capsular deposits to aid in achieving permanent clear vision. He finally sutures the cut and places antibiotic solution into the eye. This procedure does not include endoscopic cyclophotocoagulation in which a laser is used to destroy the ciliary body to treat glaucoma. Terminology Amblyogenic developmental stage: Phase during early visual development in which the visual system is at risk to develop abnormal vision. Capsule of the eye: Clear, membranous, and elastic structure in the lens of the eye. Capsulorrhexis: Technique to remove the lens capsule during a cataract surgery involving a continuous circular tear of the anterior lens capsule. Cataract: A clouding or opacity of the lens in the eyes that leads to a gradual loss of vision over time. Intraocular: Within the eyeball. Iris expansion device: Device used to dilate the eye during cataract surgery. Nucleus (of eye lens): Central innermost part of the eye lens. Phacoemulsification: Cataract surgery involving the use of an ultrasonic device to remove cloudiness from the eye. Prosthesis (pl. prostheses): An artificial or man–made replacement for a body part; also known as a prosthetic or prosthetic device; also, a device to augment an impaired body part, such as a penile prosthesis. Tips Report temporary code 0308T if the provider inserts an ocular telescope prosthesis, which is a tiny telescopic eye implant, and removes the crystalline lens. Extracapsular extraction involves removal of the eye lens leaving the posterior capsule mostly intact whereas intracapsular extraction entails the removal of both lens and surrounding lens capsule. lay_term: The provider inserts an intraocular lens prosthesis during the same session as extracapsular cataract extraction using complex techniques and devices. The provider also inserts one or more anterior segment aqueous drainage devices in the eye, typically to lower pressure in the eye. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, typically by application of local anesthesia to the eye, the provider makes a small incision in the eye and then enters the capsule and removes the hard nucleus from the lens of the eye. The provider may use an iris expansion device to aid in achieving stable dilation of the pupil and then evacuates the soft lens cortex, leaving the capsule partially intact. The provider uses magnification to assist with visualization. The provider inserts a prosthetic intraocular lens after a technique such as irrigation and aspiration (I&A). The provider also may use phacoemulsification, using an ultrasonic device to break up the cloudy lens and then using I&A to remove it from the eye before inserting an intraocular lens prosthesis. The provider also may provide support to an intraocular lens by suturing it behind the iris if the capsule support is not sufficient to hold the lens. The provider also might employ primary posterior capsulorrhexis (making a circular tear of the capsule) to remove posterior capsular deposits to aid in achieving permanent clear vision. To insert the drainage device, the provider typically uses a needle–like delivery device to enter the anterior segment (the front–most region of the eye). The provider inserts the small drainage device into the trabecular meshwork, which is tissue that drains most of the thick watery substance called aqueous fluid from the eye. The fluid goes into a circular drainage canal in the eye called Schlemm’s canal. The provider may place one or more drainage devices during the session. Providers may insert the drainage devices to help reduce pressure in the eye, such as in patients with glaucoma. The provider closes the surgical wounds and places antibiotic solution into the eye. Terminology Amblyogenic developmental stage: The phase during early visual development in which the visual system is at risk to develop abnormal vision. Anterior chamber of eye: The space between the cornea and the iris that contains aqueous humor, a thick watery substance, and communicates through the pupil with the posterior chamber at the back of the eye. Capsule of lens: Clear, membranous, and elastic structure around the lens of the eye. Capsulorrhexis: Technique to remove the lens capsule during a cataract surgery involving a continuous circular tear of the anterior lens capsule. Cataract: A clouding or opacity of the lens in the eyes that leads to a gradual loss of vision over time. Glaucoma: Eye disorder characterized by increased intraocular pressure, the pressure caused by the fluid inside the eye, the aqueous humor, that helps maintain the shape of the eye. Intraocular lens (IOL): A surgically implanted artificial lens that replaces a cloudy or opacified lens, or cataract; IOLs come in specific diopter strengths, or powers, allowing near or far vision; a multifocal lens allows both near and far vision. Iris expansion device: A surgical instrument such as an iris hook, pupil dilator or expander rings, or iris retractors that a provider uses to dilate the eye during cataract surgery. Nucleus (of eye lens): Central innermost part of the eye lens. Phacoemulsification: A technique in which the provider uses an ultrasonic device to fragment the cloudy lens (cataract) to improve the vision; also known as phacofragmentation. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, typically under local anesthesia into the area around the eye socket, the provider makes a small incision in the eye and then enters the capsule and removes the hard nucleus from the lens of the eye. He may use an iris expansion device for the procedure as this will aid in achieving stable dilation of the pupil. He then evacuates the soft lens cortex, leaving the capsule partially intact. He uses a microscope to assist with visualization. He stabilizes the anterior chamber and deepens the ciliary sulcus with an ophthalmic viscoelastic device, such as Healon GV. He inserts a laser endoscope that contains an image guide, a light source, and a laser probe into the eye and visualizes the ciliary body epithelium. He continuously visualizes the movement of the laser probe and records the images using a video camera. Once he switches the probe on, the laser beam falls on the ciliary process which whitens and shrinks to reduce the intraocular pressure. He uses the video monitor to regulate the damage to the ciliary body. Using a capsulotomy needle or capsulorrhexis forceps, the provider makes a central linear cut in the anterior capsule. He pushes or pulls a needle from the end of the cut in the direction of the desired tear. This allows the anterior capsule to fold over upon itself. The provider then completes the capsulorrhexis in a circular manner directing the tension toward the center of the lens. The provider may use irrigation and aspiration (I&A) or phacoemulsification, in which he uses an ultrasonic device to break up the cloudy lens, and then I&A to remove the lens from the eye. He then inserts the intraocular lens prosthesis. The provider may also provide support to an intraocular lens by suturing it behind the iris if the capsule support is not sufficient to hold the lens. lay_term: The provider removes most of the vitreous humor, the gelatinous material that gives shape to the eye, to provide access to the retina or to remove material within the vitreous that obstructs vision. He accesses the vitreous anteriorly, or from the front of the eye, through the limbus or cornea, and uses mechanical tools to remove the vitreous. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a small incision in the cornea. He inserts a cutting tool, like a vitrector, through the juncture of cornea and sclera or uses an open sky technique which involves the passage of tools through the cornea to the vitreous cavity. He uses the tool to mechanically excise the vitreous material. The provider further aspirates most of the vitreous humor from the eye. lay_term: The provider injects a vitreous substitute, such as gas, silicone, or a spreading agent into the eye to replace vitreous that a provider removes during a procedure, or to maintain or regain intraocular pressure. Explanation The vitreous humor is the semifluid substance that fills the region between the lens and the retina of the eye. The provider sterilizes the injection site, checks the intraocular pressure along with pupillary dilation, or enlarging the pupils, and applies topical anesthesia. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider begins by placing an ocular speculum into the patient's eye. The provider then inserts the needle through the pars plana or limbus with the tip aimed towards the center of the globe, or eyeball, to avoid any contact with the posterior lens. The provider slowly injects the vitreous substitute and then slowly and carefully removes the needle. The provider may use a sterile, cotton–tipped applicator to prevent reflux and to steady the eye. Finally, the provider applies antibiotics and transfers the patient to a recovery room. Terminology Aqueous: Thick watery substance filling the space between the lens and the cornea. Aspiration: Removal of a substance such as air, fluid, or tissue from a cavity or organ, such as the lung, using suction. Intraocular pressure (IOP): The pressure created inside the eye by the eye fluid's continual production and drainage. Lens: Transparent eye structure that focuses light onto the retina. Limbus: The junction of the cornea of the eye where it is continuous with the sclera. Ocular speculum: A small, lightweight surgical instrument used to hold the eye open during a procedure. Pars plana: Darkly pigmented posterior area of the ciliary body, the structure that lies just behind the iris, and produces the aqueous fluid for the eye. Retina: Light sensitive layers of tissue present at the back of the inner eye. Vitreous substitute: Substance used to replace the vitreous body, or the clear, jellylike substance that fills the space between the lens and the retina in the eye and through which light passes. Tips For injection of anti–inflammatory agents, antibiotics, and anticoagulants look to 67028. When the provider performs this service as part of another procedure, do not report 67028 along with the code for the inclusive procedure. However, when the provider performs a vitreous injection as the sole procedure, then report 67028. Read Less

short_description: Implantation of intravitreal drug delivery system (eg, ganciclovir implant), includes concomitant removal of vitreous Notes: (For removal, use 67121)
lay_term: The provider removes a portion of vitreous humor and inserts an implant containing a slow–release medication into the vitreous cavity of the eye so as to have a consistent supply of a drug to the affected area of the eye, for treatment of a condition like retinitis due to cytomegalovirus. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider places an ocular speculum in the patient's eye. He makes an incision at the border of the cornea and the sclera and opens the conjunctiva inferotemporally, or toward the lower lateral, or side, quadrant of the eye. The provider then uses a vitreous cutter to remove a portion of the vitreous humor. Later, he implants a small pellet of a drug like ganciclovir through the wound into the vitreous cavity and fixes its position with sutures. Finally, he sutures the incision, restores the pressure of the eye, examines the retina for any breaks, and administers subconjunctival antibiotics. Terminology Cornea: Front portion of the eye that refracts, or focuses, incoming light. Conjunctiva: The transparent membrane covering the front of the eye and lining the eyelids. Cytomegalovirus retinitis: A viral infection in the retina that occurs primarily in people whose immune systems are weakened; untreated, the disease leads to blindness. Ganciclovir implant: A slow–release formulation of a potent antiviral medication for implantation in the vitreous of the eye. Intraocular: Within the eye. Intravitreal drug delivery system: Method of delivering medication directly into the vitreous chamber through an implant that releases a specific amount of the drug over time. Ocular speculum: A small, lightweight surgical instrument used to hold the eye open during a procedure. Posterior: Closer to the back of the body or a structure. Retina: Sensory membrane in the back of the eye, which contains cells called rods and cones that receive light impulses from the lens of the eye; it sends the impulse signals to the brain, which allows the person to see. Sclera: Thick, fibrous, white, outer covering of the eyeball. Subconjunctival: Below the conjunctiva, the transparent membrane covering the front of the eye and lining the eyelids. Vitreous cavity: Space between the lens and the retina that contains vitreous humor, a clear gel fluid that helps to maintain the shape of the eye. Vitrectomy: Surgical excision of the vitreous, the gelatinous substance in the eye. Vitreous, or vitreous humor: The gelatinous, transparent substance that fills the center of the eye between the lens and the retina. Tips This procedure includes a vitrectomy. Do not separately report the vitrectomy portion of the procedure. Use the appropriate HCPCS code for the implant. Use code 67121, Removal of implanted material, posterior segment; intraocular, for removal of the implant. Read Less

short_description: Intravitreal injection of a pharmacologic agent (separate procedure)
lay_term: The provider injects a medication into the vitreous chamber of the eye as an isolated procedure or a separate procedure unrelated to any other procedure being performed on the eye. Explanation The ophthalmologist sterilizes the injection site, checks the intraocular pressure along with papillary dilation, and applies topical anesthesia. The intravitreal agent is drawn into a syringe. Before administration, care is taken to ensure no air bubbles remain in the syringe as that would have negative consequences. The needle is then introduced into the middle of the vitreous cavity, aiming posterior and slightly inferior; the drug is administered slowly into the eye. After administration, the needle is removed slowly. If necessary, indirect ophthalmoscopy is performed to ensure the correct placement of the medication. Finally, antibiotics are applied and the patient is transferred to a recovery room. Terminology Ophthalmoscopy: Examination of the internal surfaces of the hollow eye cavity through a dilated pupil; in indirect ophthalmoscopy, the machine produces an inverted image of the fundus of the eye. Vitrectomy: Surgical method to remove some or all of the vitreous humor, a semifluid substance that fills the region between the lens and the retina of the eye. Vitreous humor: Watery fluid behind the lens of the eye. Tips The descriptor for this code indicates that the procedure is a separate procedure and should not be reported when performed along with a related procedure (e.g., same anatomic area or through the same incision, orifice, or surgical approach). If the provider performs this procedure with an unrelated procedure, append modifier 59, Distinct procedural service to the code. Be sure the documentation supports the procedure as a separate procedure and not part of some other related procedure. Do not append modifier 59 when a more specific modifier, such as XE (same date, separate encounter), XP (different practitioner), XS (separate organ or structure), or XU (service does not overlap with the usual components of the main service). Documentation must support the use of the modifier. Do not confuse modifier 59 with modifier 51 for multiple procedures (e.g., same procedure on different anatomic sites, related procedures on the same anatomic site, or the same procedure multiple times on the same anatomic site). Additional Info An intravitreal injection is the process of injecting a medication into the vitreous humor (watery fluid behind the lens of the eye). The vitreous humor is the semifluid substance that fills the region between the lens and the retina of the eye. Conditions such as macular degeneration and other diseases of the retina and eye can be treated with an injection of drugs into the vitreous humor. Drugs can also be delivered at regular intervals through small capsular implants that are inserted into the eye. Improper delivery can result in complications including infection, vitreous hemorrhage, retinal detachment, and traumatic cataract. Therefore the ophthalmologist needs to take extreme precaution and care while administering an intravitreal injection. Read Less

short_description: Severing of vitreous strands, vitreous face adhesions, sheets, membranes or opacities, laser surgery (1 or more stages)
lay_term: The provider uses a laser to remove vitreous material that is obstructing a patient’s vision. Explanation The vitreous humor is the semi liquid substance that fills the region between the lens and the retina of the eye. The provider uses a YAG laser to destroy protein and detached vitreous matter in the eye that is obstructing a patient’s vision. In this procedure, the provider begins by fully dilating and examining the eye and then applying a topical anesthetic. The provider then places a special contact lens on the patient’s cornea, the transparent membrane of the outer layer of eyeball. Using a YAG laser, the provider starts the treatment anteriorly and proceeds inwards moving from the top down to maintain a clear view of the structures to be treated. The provider starts with a single burst of energy to begin removing vitreous matter, being careful to stay away from the lens and the retina. He continues the destruction of the vitreous material that is obstructing the patient’s vision. Often more than one treatment session is necessary. Terminology Adhesions: Vitreous that is adhered to the retina that has partially separated from the retina. Lens: Transparent eye structure that focuses light onto the retina. Opacities: Small clumps of protein that develop as vitreous breaks down, which does not allow light to pass through it. Retina: Light sensitive layers of tissue present at the back of inner eye. YAG laser: A surgical laser producing a short pulsed, high energy light beam to incise, perforate, or disintegrate tissue. Tips 67031 is bundled with vitrectomy procedures. Since codes 67036 to 67043 already include removing the vitreous, other codes for removing or dissecting small areas or amounts of vitreous, like 67031, are bundled with them. Read Less

short_description: Vitrectomy, mechanical, pars plana approach
lay_term: The provider removes vitreous fluid from the eye to access the posterior segment of the eye and introduce surgical instruments through incisions in the pars plana. Explanation The vitreous humor is the semi liquid substance that fills the region between the lens and the retina of the eye. In this procedure, the provider removes this substance to gain surgical access to the back of the eye. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider places a special contact lens on the patient’s cornea, the transparent membrane of the outer layer of eyeball. The provider may use different types of vitrectomy equipment to incise the eye to expose the sclera and make incisions about the entire circumference of the cornea. Regardless of the equipment, the provider makes three small incisions to insert a lighted cannula, an infusion cannula, and cutting and suction instruments. Once the instruments are in place, the provider removes the vitreous from the eye, often referred to as a posterior sclerotomy. Finally, he removes the instrumentation and closes the incision in layers using sutures. He may inject a sterile solution into the eye to restore pressure. He may also apply a pressure patch with an antibiotic ointment. Terminology Aspiration: Removal of substance such as air, fluid, or tissue from a cavity or organ, such as the lung, using suction. Cannula: A tube that a provider inserts into the body to draw off fluid or to introduce medication. Lens: Transparent eye structure that focuses light onto the retina. Lensectomy: Removal of the lens of the eye. Ophthalmic endoscope: A lighted, optical instrument for the visualization of the interior of the eye. Pars plana: The darkly pigmented posterior area of the ciliary body, the structure that lies just behind the iris, and produces the aqueous fluid for the eye. Phacofragmentation, or phacoemulsification: A technique in which the provider uses an ultrasonic device to fragment the cloudy lens, or cataract, to improve the vision. Posterior segment: Back part of the eye. Retina: Light sensitive layers of tissue present at the back of inner eye. Sclera: White of the eye. Vitrectomy: Surgical removal of vitreous humor. Vitrector: Equipment used to perform a vitrectomy, having a probe that can irrigate, aspirate, or cut. Tips Report 67036 if the lens material has dropped to the back of the posterior chamber, making a posterior vitrectomy necessary. If the lens material is small, and the provider removes it with a vitrector, do not report a separate code for its removal. If the lens material is large and requires phacofragmentation to remove it, report 66850, Removal of lens material; phacofragmentation technique, mechanical or ultrasonic, e.g., phacoemulsification, with aspiration; and 67036 for the pars plana vitrectomy. However, if the lens material is not far from its original position, and only a partial posterior vitrectomy is necessary to remove it, report 66852, Removal of lens material; pars plana approach, with or without vitrectomy, which includes both the vitrectomy and lensectomy. Code 67036 may require the use of the ophthalmic endoscope to visualize of parts of the eye not visible with an operating microscope. In this situation, use add–on code 66990 in addition to 67036. short_description: Vitrectomy, mechanical, pars plana approach; with focal endolaser photocoagulation
lay_term: The provider removes vitreous humor from the eye to access the posterior segment of the eye and introduce surgical instruments through incisions in the pars plana. This procedure also includes the treatment of small localized areas for retinal conditions. Explanation The vitreous humor is the semi liquid substance that fills the region between the lens and the retina of the eye. In this procedure, the provider removes this substance to gain surgical access to the back of the eye. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider places a special contact lens on the patient’s cornea, the transparent membrane of the outer layer of eyeball. The provider may use different types of vitrectomy equipment to incise the eye to expose the sclera and make incisions about the entire circumference of the cornea. Regardless of the equipment, the provider makes three small incisions to insert a lighted cannula, an infusion cannula, and cutting and suction instruments. Once the instruments are in place, the provider removes the vitreous from the eye, often referred to as a posterior sclerotomy. In this procedure, the provider also uses a focal treatment to address conditions such as leaking microaneurysms in the eye which diabetes caused. These retinal microvascular changes result in macular edema, or retinal thickening. The provider treats the areas of leakage identified by using an endolaser, or a laser probe. The provider positions the laser in the vitreous cavity, applies the laser light directly to the retina, coagulating or causing the blood to clot and seal off the bleeding blood vessels. This procedure effectively stops or slows the leakage of blood and fluid in the eye, as the abnormal blood vessels are closed by the laser burns. Once the procedure is complete, the provider removes the instrumentation and closes the incision using layered sutures. He may inject a sterile solution into the eye to restore pressure. He may also apply a pressure patch with an antibiotic ointment. Terminology Cannula: A tube that a provider inserts into the body to draw off fluid or to introduce medication. Focal endolaser photocoagulation: Use of a focused laser light to coagulate tissue or seal blood vessels in small areas of tissue. Lens: Transparent eye structure that focuses light onto the retina. Microaneurysm: A microscopic aneurysm, or minute swelling in a blood vessel wall. Pars plana: The darkly pigmented posterior area of the ciliary body, the structure that lies just behind the iris, and produces the aqueous fluid for the eye. Posterior segment: Back part of the eye. Retina: Light sensitive layers of tissue present at the back of inner eye. Sclera: White of the eye. Sclerotomy: Surgical incision of the sclera. Vitrectomy: Surgical removal of vitreous humor. short_description: Vitrectomy, mechanical, pars plana approach; with endolaser panretinal photocoagulation
lay_term: The provider removes vitreous humor from the eye to access the posterior segment of the eye and introduce surgical instruments through incisions in the pars plana. This procedure also includes the treatment of retinal diseases affecting a larger area of the retina. Explanation The vitreous humor is the semi liquid substance that fills the region between the lens and the retina of the eye. In this procedure, the provider removes this substance to gain surgical access to the back of the eye. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider places a special contact lens on the patient’s cornea, the transparent membrane of the outer layer of eyeball. The provider may use different types of vitrectomy equipment to incise the eye to expose the sclera and make incisions about the entire circumference of the cornea. Regardless of the equipment, the provider makes three small incisions to insert a lighted cannula, and an infusion cannula, and cutting and suction instruments. Once the instruments are in place, the provider removes the vitreous from the eye, often referred to as a posterior sclerotomy. In this procedure, the provider also uses a panretinal laser treatment to address proliferative diseases, or diseases which grow and increase rapidly, such as diabetic retinopathy. The provider treats the areas of blood vessel blockage and abnormal blood vessel growth by using an endolaser, or a laser probe. This strong laser places multiple, scatter laser burns in the areas of retinal leakage, and the burn scars cause the abnormal blood vessels to shrink; this also may prevent retinal detachment by helping to bond the retina to the back of the eye. Once the procedure is complete, the provider removes the instrumentation and closes the incision using sutures. He may inject a sterile solution into the eye to restore pressure. He may also apply a pressure patch with an antibiotic ointment. Terminology Cannula: A tube that a provider inserts into the body to draw off fluid or to introduce medication. Diabetic retinopathy: A complication of diabetes that affects the retina of the eye, causing blockages of the blood vessels and subsequent abnormal blood vessel growth. Endolaser panretinal photocoagulation: Use of multiple, strong laser lights to coagulate tissue or seal blood vessels in large areas of tissue; also known as scatter laser treatment. Lens: Transparent eye structure that focuses light onto the retina. Pars plana: The darkly pigmented posterior area of the ciliary body, the structure that lies just behind the iris, and produces the aqueous fluid for the eye Posterior segment: Back part of the eye. Retina: Light sensitive layers of tissue present at the back of inner eye. Retinal detachment: A medical condition in which the retina is separated from its attachment to the supporting layers within the eye. Sclera: White of the eye. Vitrectomy: Surgical removal of vitreous humor. Read Less

short_description: Vitrectomy, mechanical, pars plana approach; with removal of internal limiting membrane of retina (eg, for repair of macular hole, diabetic macular edema), includes, if performed, intraocular tamponade (ie, air, gas or silicone oil)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider removes vitreous humor, the gelatinous material that gives shape to the eye, using a mechanical cutting tool. He removes the internal limiting membrane of the retina to treat swelling of the macula or repair a hole in the macula. He may also inject air, gas, or silicone oil to stabilize the retina. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision through the pars plana. He inserts a mechanical cutting instrument through the incision and removes vitreous humor from the eye. The provider also inserts intraocular micro forceps, a small grasping instrument that helps to lift the edges of the internal limiting membrane of the retina. He elevates it and permanently removes it. Next, he stabilizes the retina by injecting air, gas, or silicone oil. Finally, he closes the incision with sutures, administers a topical antibiotic to the eye, and applies an eye pressure patch. Terminology Antibiotic: Substance that inhibits infection. Diabetic macular edema: Excessive swelling of the macula, the yellow central part of retina responsible for central vision, due to fluid retention as a result of diabetes. Internal limiting membrane: A thin layer of scar tissue on the eye's macula that distorts the retina and impairs vision; also known as epiretinal membrane, cellophane retinopathy, or macular pucker. Intraocular tamponade: Injection of a substance, such as air, gas or oil, to stabilize the retina. Macular hole: Small tear in the macula, the yellow central part of retina responsible for central vision. Pars plana: A structure in the middle of the eye, between the retina and the iris, a common access point for excision of the vitreous, which is the gelatinous substance in the eye. Retina: Sensory membrane in the back of the eye, which contains cells called rods and cones that receive light impulses from the lens of the eye; it sends the impulse signals to the brain, which allow the person to see. Vitrectomy: Surgical excision of the vitreous, the gelatinous substance in the eye. Vitreous, or vitreous humor: The gelatinous, transparent substance that fills the center of the eye between the lens and the retina. Vitreous substitute: Replacement material to retain the shape and volume of the vitreous cavity when vitreous has been removed, such as air, gas, salt solution, silicone oil, or other chemicals with properties that mimic the vitreous. Tips If the provider injects a vitreous substitute, check with your payer before reporting it separately. Read Less

lay_term: In this procedure, the provider removes vitreous humor, the gelatinous material that gives shape to the eye, using a mechanical cutting tool. He then removes the subretinal membrane to treat excessive growth of new vessels that obstruct the vision, common in age related macular degeneration. He may also use air, gas or silicone oil to stabilize the retina and employ a laser beam to heal the damaged retinal tissues, if present. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision through the pars plana. He then inserts a mechanical cutting tool and removes vitreous humor from the eye. The provider also makes an incision in the retina and inserts subretinal forceps, a grasping instrument, to elevate, gently peel, and remove the subretinal membrane from the eye. Explanation The provider performs a procedure on the posterior segment of the eye that is not represented by any of the standard and active CPT® codes available. When reporting a procedure with an unlisted code, submit a cover letter explaining the reason for choosing the unlisted code instead of a defined, active code. short_description: Conjunctivoplasty; with conjunctival graft or extensive rearrangement
lay_term: The provider performs a surgical repair of the conjunctiva using the patient’s own conjunctival tissue as a graft or by rearranging the existing tissue. This procedure is done to treat a condition such as conjunctivochalasis, a common painful condition caused by excess folds of conjunctiva in the eye. Explanation The conjunctiva is the tissue lining that covers the inside of the eyelids and the eyeball. In this service, the provider removes a portion of the conjunctival tissue on the eyeball to relax folded conjunctival tissue and create a graft for repair of the wound. The provider performs the surgery with the patient under a local anesthetic and appropriately prepped and draped. She then identifies the most relaxed areas of loose conjunctiva using an operating microscope or loupe magnification. Next, she excises a small strip of conjunctiva from the underlying tissue to allow relaxation of the loose tissue away from the cornea. She does this taking care to leave enough healthy conjunctiva adjacent to the cornea. The provider may be able to suture or glue the conjunctival margins together by extensively rearranging the existing tissue to close the wound. Otherwise, the provider prepares the wound location for the graft and trims the harvested tissue to the same size as the defect making the graft a little larger on all side except the corneal side. She then sutures or uses a tissue adhesive to secure the graft underneath the conjunctiva. When the procedure is complete, she applies a pressure patch with antibiotic ointment. Terminology Loupe magnification: A magnifying eyepiece used to see small details more closely. Tips CPT® provides one modifier for each eyelid: E1 for upper left, E2 for lower left, E3 for upper right, and E4 for lower right. short_description: Radical excision external auditory canal lesion; without neck dissection
lay_term: The provider excises an extensive lesion of the external ear canal along with surrounding structures. He performs this procedure when a lesion becomes metastatic and starts invading other anatomical structures, which are near to, or adjacent to, the external ear. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider approaches the external ear canal through an incision behind the ear. He extends the incision to the front of the ear and all the way to the parotid, or salivary, gland in the cheek. He dissects around surrounding structures. Depending on the extent of the lesion, the provider excises not just the external ear canal but the parotid gland; the tympanic membrane, or eardrum; and the ear bones, i.e., the malleus or hammer, the incus or anvil, and the stapes or stirrup. The excision may also include a portion of the facial nerve and nearby supporting structures, e.g., part of the lower jaw bone and temporal bone protrusion. He removes all these structures en bloc, or all together rather than piecemeal. When he determines that he has excised all the affected structures that can safely be excised, he closes the incision in layers. Depending on the extent of the excision, he may need to use a graft for complete closure. If so, he harvests the graft from another area and closes that incision site. He places the graft over the area and secures it with sutures. He packs the ear with gauze soaked in antibiotic solution and covers the ear with a dressing. This procedure does not involve neck dissection. Terminology Cholesteatoma: A benign tumor of the ear that often contains cholesterol, an important lipid, or steroid, component of all cells. Epithelial: Pertaining to the epithelium, the outermost tissue layer on all structures of the body. Excision: Removal of tissue, organ, or other structure in whole or in part; also resection. External auditory canal: The portion of the ear canal from the opening to the eardrum or tympanic membrane. External auditory canal: The portion of the ear canal from the opening to the eardrum or tympanic membrane. Harvest: Remove skin, a portion of a vessel, bone, or other tissue from a patient or donor, generally to be used for grafting or anastomosis. Lipoma: A fatty tumor, typically occurring in the subcutaneous tissue but may be found in the deeper soft tissues. Metastatic: Pertaining to metastasis, the spread of cancer to other parts of the body from its original site. Parotid gland, or salivary gland: One of three glands in the cheek that secrete a fluid that provides moisture for chewing and also begins the process of breaking down the food; parotid literally means near or beside the ear. Radical excision: Surgical removal of a structure to include its vascular supply, associated lymph nodes if present, and a sufficient margin of surrounding tissues, especially around a tumor, to ensure that all diseased tissue is removed; also called radical resection. Resection: Surgical removal of tissue, organ, or other structure in whole or in part; also called excision. Sebaceous cyst: Benign, or noncancerous, growth beneath the surface of the skin consisting of a sac filled with oily material. Temporal bone: A bone at the base and side of the skull that houses the tympanic membrane and part of the incus and malleus; the three parts of the bone are referred to as the petrous bone, the squamous bone, and the tympanic bone; it also includes the styloid process, a projection off the inferior surface where several muscles and ligaments attach. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a postauricular incision and extends it along the posterior and inferior conchal borders and the posterior ear canal meatus. He resects the conchal cartilage and dissects the underlying soft tissue to create an enlarged meatus. He may need to remove bone from the floor of the canal to enlarge the opening. He raises a flap of conchal skin medially and fuses to the soft tissue on the deep surface of the pinna with sutures. He rotates the flap of posterior canal skin and sutures it to the skin edge of the inferior conchal gap. If necessary, he may place a graft using tissue harvested from another location to complete the repair. He places antibiotic ointment through the meatus into the ear canal. He repairs the incision behind the ear with interrupted sutures and applies a dressing over the ear. Terminology Antibiotic: Substance that inhibits infection. External auditory canal: The portion of the ear canal from the opening to the eardrum or tympanic membrane. Canalplasty: Reconstruction, using plastic repair techniques, of a passage such as the external auditory canal. Conchal: The part of the external ear that looks like a conch shell. Harvest: Remove skin, a portion of a vessel, bone, or other tissue from a patient or donor, generally to be used for grafting or anastomosis. Mastoidectomy: A mastoidectomy can include a simple opening up of the cortex or outer covering of the mastoid cavity or excision of all the mastoid air cells and surrounding structures. Meatoplasty: Plastic reconstruction of the meatus. Meatus: The opening of the ear canal; the external meatus consists primarily of cartilage while the internal meatus consists partly of bone. Ossicular chain: The three ossicles, or bones, of the inner ear that vibrate and transmit sound to the eardrum or tympanic membrane; named for shapes they resemble, the bones consist of the malleus or hammer, the incus or anvil, and the stapes or stirrup. Pinna: The outer ear, also called the auricle or auricula. Postauricular: Behind the ear. Radical: Directed at the root cause of a problem; in surgery, often used synonymously with major or extensive. Tympanic membrane: The eardrum, the structure between the external and internal ear canal that vibrates and transmits sound. Tympanoplasty: Surgical repair of the eardrum. Tips Report this code only when the documentation supports a canalplasty, such as drilling the bony canal or attaching skin grafts. CPT® designates 69310 as a separate procedure, which means you can bill this procedure only if it is the only procedure the provider provides in a given anatomical area. CPT® automatically includes 69310 in any more extensive procedure provided in the same area during the same operative session, such as 69646, Tympanoplasty with mastoidectomy, including canalplasty, middle ear surgery, tympanic membrane repair; radical or complete, with ossicular chain reconstruction. short_description: Myringotomy including aspiration and/or eustachian tube inflation
lay_term: The provider makes a small incision in the eardrum (myringotomy); he may suck fluid from the middle ear (aspiration) and/or inject air through a tube or catheter placed through the tympanotomy to inflate the eustachian tube (ET) to treat ET dysfunction or otitis media. Explanation With the patient appropriately prepped and using topical anesthesia, the provider treats auditory tube dysfunction or otitis media by making a small cut in the tympanic membrane and dilating the eustachian tube. He may also aspirate serous fluid or effusion from the tympanic cavity and/or insert a tube through the tympanotomy and inflate the eustachian tube. Terminology Aspiration: Removal of fluid, gas, or other material through a tube attached to a suction device, often for laboratory analysis or combined with irrigation, the instillation of fluid to clean a wound or to wash out a cavity such as the abdomen, stomach, lungs, or joints; also, breathing in or sucking in food, fluid, or a foreign object into the airway. Eustachian tube: The narrow passageway that leads from the middle ear to the nasopharynx, also known as the auditory tube or pharyngotympanic tube. Tympanotomy: Incision into the tympanic membrane (eardrum) typically to relieve pressure or to drain pus from an infection in the middle ear. Tips This code is for when the provider performs myringotomy under local or topical anesthesia. When the provider performs the same procedure with the patient under general anesthesia, see 69421. For a laser–assisted myringotomy, see S2225. This code may not be accepted by all payers. For balloon dilation of the Eustachian tube via nasopharyngoscopy, see 69705 and 69706. For a tympanostomy and insertion of a ventilation tube under local or topical anesthesia, see 64933, and for the same procedure under general anesthesia, see 64936. Read Less

short_description: Petrous apicectomy including radical mastoidectomy
lay_term: The provider removes the top of the petrous portion of the temporal bone to treat disorders like acute petrositis, impaired mobility of malleus, and cholesteatoma or cholesteatosis of the middle ear and mastoid. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision behind the ear or inside the ear canal. He extends the incision down to the mastoid air space. The provider uses an operating microscope or loupes, i.e., magnifying lenses, attached to glasses or a headband to facilitate microdissection. Using a chisel or drill, he excises the mastoid air cells and exposes the sinus and bony roof over the mastoid cavity. He does not enter the wall of the posterior ear canal. He examines the inner ear structures. He excises inflamed mucosa of the auditory tube and middle ear, debrides granulomas and cholesteatomas if present, and removes the ossicles, leaving the stapes if possible. He dissects tissues to reach the petrous bone and, again using a drill or chisel, removes the apex and the mastoid process of the temporal bone. He also performs a meatoplasty. He may irrigate the area with antibiotic solution or instill antibiotic drops. Finally, he controls any bleeding, places a drain, and closes the incision in layers. He applies a dressing over the ear. Terminology Antibiotic: Substance that inhibits infection. Cholesteatoma: A benign tumor of the ear that often contains cholesterol, an important lipidlike steroid component of all cells. Cholesteatosis: Deposits of cholesterol, an important lipidlike steroid component of all cells, in tissues. Malleus: One of the ossicles of the ear; it vibrates against the eardrum to transmit sound. Mastoid cavity: An air space, similar to a sinus cavity, except that it has septations, or walls, somewhat like a honey comb; it is located in the temporal bone above the area of the tympanic membrane. Mastoidectomy: A mastoidectomy can include a simple opening up of the cortex or outer covering of the mastoid cavity or radical resection of all the mastoid air cells and surrounding structures. Meatoplasty: Plastic reconstruction of the meatus. Ossicles: The three ear bones that vibrate and transmit sound to the eardrum or tympanic membrane; named for shapes they resemble, the bones consist of the malleus or hammer, the incus or anvil, and the stapes or stirrup. Petrositis: Inflammation of the petrous part of the temporal bone at its junction with the base of the skull; the petrous bone is dense and shaped like a pyramid. Petrous apicectomy: Excision of the top of the petrous bone, which surrounds the organ of hearing. Radical excision: Surgical removal of a structure to include its vascular supply, associated lymph nodes if present, and a sufficient margin of surrounding tissues, especially around a tumor, to ensure that all diseased tissue is removed; also called radical resection. Resection: Surgical removal of tissue, organ, or other structure in whole or in part; also called excision. Sinus: An air space, typically surrounded by bone. Temporal bone: A bone at the base and side of the skull that houses the tympanic membrane and part of the incus and malleus; the three parts of the bone are referred to as the petrous bone, the squamous bone, and the tympanic bone; it also includes the styloid process, a projection off the inferior surface where several muscles and ligaments attach. short_description: Resection temporal bone, external approach Notes: (For middle fossa approach, see 69950-69970)
lay_term: The provider uses an external ear approach to resect the temporal bone, which forms the lower side and base of the cranium, to treat cancer that spread to the skull and facial bones. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the external ear. He dissects through bone and tissues and creates auricle flaps from the external ear. Techniques and the amount of dissection necessary varies according to the extent of the cancer. The provider uses an operating microscope or loupes, i.e., magnifying lenses, attached to glasses or a headband to facilitate microdissection. The procedure may include resection of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, removal of one or more of the ossicles, a parotidectomy, mastoidectomy, neck dissection, and resection of the seventh cranial nerve. He tries to spare the stapes. He exposes the temporal bone and ultimately excises the temporal bone. Repair may include separately reportable tissue grafts and or bone grafts harvested from a separate area. Finally, the provider controls any bleeding and closes the incisions in layers. Dissection: Separation of tissues; blunt dissection involves separation of tissue layers using the fingers; sharp dissection separates tissue layers using a blade. Stapes: One of the three ossicles, or ear bones, that vibrate in response to sound. Temporal bone: A bone at the base and side of the skull that houses the tympanic membrane and part of the incus and malleus; the three parts of the bone are referred to as the petrous bone, the squamous bone, and the tympanic bone; it also includes the styloid process, a projection off the inferior surface where several muscles and ligaments attach. short_description: Excision aural glomus tumor; transmastoid
lay_term: The provider removes an aural glomus tumor using an approach through the mastoid cavity. He performs the procedure to relieve pain caused by the tumor. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision behind the ear to access the mastoid cavity. He uses a drill to clear out the cavity. The provider uses an operating microscope or loupes, i.e., magnifying lenses, attached to glasses or a headband to facilitate microdissection. He exposes the mastoid sinus posteriorly and exposes the tegmen, the bony roof over the mastoid cavity, superiorly, which separates the mastoid and middle cranial fossa. The provider creates an extended facial recess to completely visualize the tumor, being careful to leave the posterior ear canal wall intact. He uses cup forceps to remove the tumor and uses absorbable packing to control the bleeding. Whenever possible, the provider leaves the ossicles undisturbed to preserve the patient's hearing. However, if the tumor is large, the provider may have to remove the ossicles and the posterior canal wall. Once the tumor is successfully removed, the provider closes the incision with sutures and applies a dressing. Terminology Forceps: Pincers or tongs used for grasping; also surgical forceps. Glomus tumor: A usually benign, painful, vascular tumor that occurs primarily in the fingers but may also appear in the nose or in the tympanic body of the jugular vein where it causes pain in the ear. Jugular vein: A vein in the neck that returns blood from the scalp, neck, and face to the heart. Mastoid cavity: An air space, similar to a sinus cavity, except that it has septations, or walls, somewhat like a honey comb; it is located in the temporal bone above the area of the tympanic membrane. Cranial fossa: The base of the skull which forms the floor of the cranial cavity and consists of the occipital, temporal, and sphenoid bones; it is divided into anterior, middle, and posterior fossae from front to back. Ossicles: The three ear bones that vibrate and transmit sound to the eardrum or tympanic membrane; named for shapes they resemble, the bones consist of the malleus or hammer, the incus or anvil, and the stapes or stirrup. Sinus: An air space, typically surrounded by bone. Transcanal approach: Surgical approach going through the skin and tissues of the external auditory canal. Transmastoid approach: Surgical approach through the mastoid cavity. Temporal bone: A bone at the base and side of the skull that houses the tympanic membrane and part of the incus and malleus; the three parts of the bone are referred to as the petrous bone, the squamous bone, and the tympanic bone; it also includes the styloid process, a projection off the inferior surface where several muscles and ligaments attach. Tips For a transcanal approach for excision of a glomus tumor, use 69550, Excision aural glomus tumor; transcanal. For more extensive excision of an aural glomus tumor using an extratemporal approach, use 69554, Excision aural glomus tumor; extended, extratemporal. Read Less

short_description: Excision aural glomus tumor; extended (extratemporal)
lay_term: The provider removes an aural glomus tumor, which entails a mastoidectomy and, in some cases, a craniotomy and removal of the parotid gland, ear canal, and or ossicles to fully extract the entire tumor. He approaches the tumor from in front of the ear. He performs the procedure to relieve pain. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in front of the ear and dissects down through subcutaneous tissues and fascia. The provider uses an operating microscope or loupes, i.e., magnifying lenses, attached to glasses or a headband to facilitate microdissection. He identifies the facial nerve, hypoglossal nerve, spinal accessory nerve, internal jugular vein and carotid artery in the neck. He removes the mastoid and exposes the jugular bulb, which he ligates inferiorly. After stripping the mastoid sinus of its attachments and surrounding tissue, he opens and packs the cavity. The provider uses absorbable packing to control the bleeding. If needed, he removes the parotid gland to enable further mobilization of the facial nerve. Depending on the size and extent of the tumor, he may also remove the ear canal and ossicles. The provider controls any bleeding, sutures the incision closed, and applies a dressing. Carotid artery: Artery in the neck that supplies blood to the head and neck. Craniotomy: Surgical incision of the skull, or cranium. Facial nerve: The seventh cranial nerve; it supplies muscles of the head, face, and neck. Fascia: Fatty or fibrous connective tissue that covers, protects, and gives support to other structures; superficial fascia is immediately below the skin; deep fascia surrounds deeper structures such as muscles, bones, nerves, and blood vessels. Glomus tumor: A usually benign, painful, vascular tumor that occurs primarily in the fingers but may also appear in the nose or in the tympanic body of the jugular vein where it causes pain in the ear. Hypoglossal nerve: The 12th cranial nerve; it is a motor nerve that controls the movement of the tongue. Jugular vein: A vein in the neck that returns blood from the scalp, neck, and face to the heart.
