Sinus: An air space, typically surrounded by bone. Sternocleidomastoid muscle: A large muscle in the neck; it rotates the head, bends the neck, and assists with inspiration, or taking a breath; it has three attachments, one to the skull behind the ear, one at the sternum, or breast bone, and the third at the clavicle, or collar bone; it comes from behind the ear, along the neck, and over the clavicle to the chest. short_description: Revision mastoidectomy; resulting in complete mastoidectomy
lay_term: The provider revises a previous simple mastoidectomy and converts it to a total mastoidectomy. He also removes diseased mastoid mucosa or cholesteatoma, if present. He performs the procedure because the prior procedure failed to produce a dry ear, which results in recurrent otitis media accompanied by accumulation of pus, eardrum perforation, and recurrent or residual hearing loss. The patient may also suffer from acute or recurrent cholesteatoma. Explanation The provider makes an incision behind the ear and carries it down through subcutaneous tissue and fascia to access the mastoid cavity. He drills out the mastoid cavity, posteriorly exposing the mastoid sinus and superiorly exposing the tegmen, the bony plate that separates the mastoid and middle cranial fossa. He leaves the posterior ear canal wall intact and ensures visibility of the semicircular canal and part of the incus. The provider removes any diseased tissue from the mastoid and any cholesteatoma present. He controls any bleeding, and sutures the incision closed, places a temporary drain if needed, and applies a dressing. Cranial fossa: The base of the skull which forms the floor of the cranial cavity and consists of the occipital, temporal, and sphenoid bones; it is divided into anterior, middle, and posterior fossae from front to back. Otitis media: Middle ear infection. Semicircular canal: A fluid filled canal in the inner ear, lined with tiny hairs called cilia; it plays an important role in balance. short_description: Revision mastoidectomy; resulting in modified radical mastoidectomy
lay_term: The provider revises a previous simple or complete mastoidectomy with a modified radical mastoidectomy. This includes removing all of the mastoid air cells, any granulation and infected tissue, and the bony partitions of the mastoid cavity. The provider also reconstructs the ear canal if needed. He performs the procedure because the prior procedure failed to produce a dry ear, which results in recurrent otitis media accompanied by accumulation of pus, eardrum perforation, and recurrent or residual hearing loss. Explanation The provider makes an incision behind the ear and carries it down through subcutaneous tissue and fascia to access the mastoid cavity, where he removes all of the mastoid air cells, any granulation tissue or infected tissue, and the bony partitions located in the mastoid cavity. He creates a tympanomeatal flap, which he reflects anteriorly. He takes the posterior and superior bony canal walls down to the level of the facial nerve. Depending on the location of the cholesteatoma, the provider may remove the ossicles. He positions the tympanomeatal flap over the facial ridge and into the mastoid cavity, maintaining some of the middle ear space. If needed, the provider reconstructs the ear canal, then packs the canal and mastoid cavity with absorbable material to control bleeding, and closes the incision with sutures. short_description: Implantation, osseointegrated implant, skull; with percutaneous attachment to external speech processor
lay_term: The provider implants a device into the skull (bone–anchored) that facilitates converting sound energy to be received by the inner ear. The implant is coupled directly to a speech processor percutaneously (through a small opening in the skin). Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision behind the ear to allow for placement of the device that treats hearing loss. The provider uses a drill to create a hole in the skull and then inserts the implant directly into the bone (osseointegrated, the bone and implant may fuse over time). short_description: Implantation or replacement of electromagnetic bone conduction hearing device in temporal bone Notes: (Replacement procedure includes removal of old device)
lay_term: The provider implants or replaces an electromagnetic bone conduction hearing device in the temporal bone. These devices operate by passing an electric current into a coil that drives an adjacent magnet attached to one of the vibratory structures of the middle ear, e.g., tympanic membrane, ossicles, or round window. The implant treats conductive hearing loss. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider creates a postauricular incision overlying the temporal bone. He dissects any tissue to access the outer skull cortex, where he drills a circular depression into the bone behind the mastoid cavity. He places the internal coil in the depression and secures it to the skull using titanium screws. If needed, he thins the subcutaneous tissue overlying the coil. The provider irrigates the area, sutures the incision closed, and applies a dressing. Terminology Cortex: The outer covering of an organ or bone, like the bark on a tree. Mastoid cavity, or mastoid antrum: An air space, similar to a sinus cavity, except that it has septations, or walls, somewhat like a honey comb; it is located in the temporal bone above the area of the tympanic membrane. Ossicles, or ossicular chain: Three tiny bones in the inner ear; when the eardrum or tympanic membrane vibrates, the vibrations transfer to the malleus or hammer, the incus or anvil, and the stapes or stirrup in that order, and then to the oval window; the bones are named for the shapes they resemble. Postauricular: Behind the ear. Round window: A membrane between the middle and inner ear; situated below the oval window, it vibrates in opposition to the oval window; also called fenestra rotunda, fenestra cochleae, or cochlear window. Subcutaneous tissue: Tissue below the surface of the skin. Temporal bone: A bone at the base and side of the skull that houses the tympanic membrane and part of the incus and malleus; the three parts of the bone are referred to as the petrous bone, the squamous bone, and the tympanic bone; it also includes the styloid process, a projection off the inferior surface where several muscles and ligaments attach. Titanium: Lightweight but extremely strong metal used in medical fixation devices and implants due to its durability and biocompatibility. Tympanic membrane: Eardrum. Tips Clinical Scenario Question: My provider performs an implantation of an electromagnetic bone conduction hearing device in the temporal bone, which has a code of 69710. However, the procedure is not exactly how we are doing it. If we are not doing all the work in the description, how should I report the procedure? Answer: If you're not doing all the components described for a code, in this case, 69710, you should append modifier 52, Reduced services, and state that you only did parts of what is described for the code. Understandably, payers do not reimburse for the parts that you're not doing, and they may ask for supporting documentation. For removal or repair of the device, report 69711, Removal or repair of electromagnetic bone conduction hearing device in temporal bone. Read Less

The physician makes an incision into the head of the patient (depending on the approach used it can be behind the ear or above the ear). He elevates the skin flap to expose the temporal muscle. He elevates the skin flap to expose the temporal muscle. The physician drills over the mastoid until the yellow bone of the otic capsule is identified. The nerve is confined in the labyrinthine segment. The physician then repairs the seventh cranial nerve through interrupted sutures. Additionally, he may perform nerve grafting or release of pressure from the nerve. Read Less

lay_term: The provider makes a surgical incision into the labyrinth (the inner ear) and instills or perfuses one or more drugs, such as a steroid or an antibiotic, through the tympanic membrane. Explanation The provider incises the posterior ear canal skin through the external ear opening and reflects the skin flap and posterior tympanic membrane forward. He visualizes the horizontal semicircular canal. Using microscopic guidance, the provider instills one or more drugs such as anti–inflammatory steroids or aminoglycoside antibiotics, into the middle ear. The incision is then repaired with sutures. Alternatively, the provider may use a transtympanic injection with a needle to instill the drugs. Tips When your otolaryngologist injects an anti–inflammatory steroid (such as Depo–Medrol®, Solu–Medrol®, or Decadron®) or an aminoglycoside (for instance, gentamicin or streptomycin) into a patient's inner ear to treat vertigo, you should report the service with 69801. However, this code should be reported only once per day as per CPT® guideline. You do not need to add modifier 52 for reduced services if the drug is injected with a needle through the tympanic membrane. You may report a separate J code for the medication used. For instance, report the anti–inflammatory steroid Decadron® with J1100, Injection, dexamethasone sodium phosphate, 1 mg. Other possibilities include Depo–Medrol® (J1020–J1040) and Solu–Medrol® (J2920, J2930). You can even report drugs such as gentamicin with J1580, Injection, Garamycin®, gentamicin, up to 80 mg. While the procedure code can be reported only once per day, you can and should submit the drug code for each injection. For instance, use J1100 with each 1 mg of Decadron® (dexamethosone sodium phosphate) injection or J1580 for any dose up to 80 mg of Garamycin® (gentamicin). Read Less

short_description: Cochlear device implantation, with or without mastoidectomy Notes: (For implantation of vestibular device, use 0725T)
lay_term: The external parts include microphone, speech processor, and a transmitter. The implant is surgically placed under the skin behind the ear. The internal parts are a receiver and stimulator which are secured in the bone underneath the skin, and an array of electrodes wound through the cochlea which send impulses to the nerves in the scala tympani and then directly to the brain through the auditory nervous system. This procedure destroys any residual hearing the patient may have in the implanted ear; which is why single ear implantation is more commonly done. Explanation The patient is placed in the supine position. The area directly behind the ear is shaved and cleaned. The provider makes a C–shaped postauricular incision with a posterosuperior extension. The incision may be made in the hairline or, alternatively, a few millimeters posterior to the postauricular sulcus. He creates a musculoperiosteal Palva flap composed of temporalis fascia, muscle, and periosteum. Then the provider drills a well for the implant and performs a cochleostomy, an opening into the cochlea. At this point the device is implanted and placed in the well. He inserts the electrode array into the scala tympani of the basal turn of the cochlea. He closes the flap completely covering the electrode and hub. A standard dressing is applied. Tips When a patient receives a cochlear implant, the audiologist must initially program the speech–generating device and then periodically adjust it. Analysis and programming of a cochlear implant is not included in 69930 (Cochlear device implantation, with or without mastoidectomy), and you can report the service separately, even during 69930's 90–day global period. Initial programming usually occurs a month or so after the implant. Follow–up adjustments may occur a dozen times or more in the first year, followed by only four adjustments in subsequent years, depending on the patient. When your audiologist provides diagnostic analysis for a patient who is younger than 7 years of age, you should report 92601 for the initial stimulation and 92602 for the follow–up programming. For patients age 7 or older, you should bill 92603 for initial stimulation and 92604 for follow–up programming. If the procedure is performed bilaterally, some payers recognize modifier 50 appended to the code reported on one line (69930–50). Other payers may prefer the code reported on two lines with the modifiers LT and RT for left and right sides. Check with the payer to confirm their preferences. Medicare's bilateral–surgery rules pay the first surgery at 100 percent and the second–side surgery at 50 percent. Check your explanation of benefits (EOB) for payment on 69930–50 to make sure the insurer paid you for the bilateral procedure. If you don't have the payer's fee schedule, compare the rate to unilateral 69930 charges to ensure you didn't receive payment for one side only. Read Less

short_description: Vestibular nerve section, transcranial approach
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider sections the vestibular nerve to disconnect a balance organ from the brain. The provider uses a transcranial approach to perform this procedure. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a vertical incision anterior to the auricle, exposing and dividing the temporal muscle. He removes a section of the patient's skull to expose the dura mater over the temporal lobe of the brain and he elevates the dura from the middle fossa. He drills until he can identify the facial nerve and follows the nerve to the internal auditory canal. He compresses the canal with the drill and incises the vestibular nerves. The provider incises the vestibular nerve but not the fascial or cochlear nerve, a branch of the auditory nerve that carries sound from the inner ear directly to the brain. He then places a muscle graft over the internal auditory canal and replaces the bone in the skull. Finally, he closes the incision with sutures and applies a dressing. Terminology Anterior: Closer to the front part of the body or a structure. Auricular: Related to the ear. Dura mater: The outer fibrous membrane just underneath the skull, the toughest of three membranes or meninges that protect the brain and spinal cord. Internal auditory canal: The narrow passageway from the outer ear to the eardrum. Temporal lobe: One of the lobes of each cerebral hemisphere located on the side and in front of the occipital lobe. Temporalis muscle: Broad muscle on the side of the head, involved in mastication, or chewing. Vestibular nerve: One branch of the eighth cranial nerve. Read Less

short_description: Total facial nerve decompression and/or repair (may include graft)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider repairs or decompresses the facial nerve and may perform a nerve graft when necessary. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a vertical incision anterior to the auricle, exposing and dividing the temporal muscle. He removes a section of the patient's skull to expose the dura mater over the temporal lobe of the brain and he elevates the dura from the middle fossa. He drills until the facial nerve is exposed. Depending upon each specific surgery, the provider may repair the nerve with sutures, graft the nerve, remove a tumor, or decompress the nerve. The provider may alternatively use a transmastoid approach if extensive compression is necessary. The provider places a muscle graft over the floor of the middle cranial fossa and replaces the bone in the skull. Finally, he sutures the incision and applies a dressing. Terminology Anterior: Closer to the front part of the body or a structure. Auricular: Related to the ear. Decompress: A procedure to relieve pressure on a structure. Dura mater: The outer fibrous membrane just underneath the skull, the toughest of three membranes or meninges that protect the brain and spinal cord. Graft: Internal auditory canal: The narrow passageway from the outer ear to the eardrum. Middle cranial fossa: The butterfly–shaped depressed area at the base of the cranial cavity where the temporal lobes of the brain and the pituitary glands reside. Temporal lobe: One of the lobes of each cerebral hemisphere located on the side and in front of the occipital lobe. Temporalis muscle: Broad muscle on the side of the head, involved in mastication, or chewing. Transmastoid: Through the mastoid. Tumor: Abnormal growth of tissue or mass, benign or cancerous. short_description: Unlisted procedure, temporal bone, middle fossa approach
lay_term: Use 69979 to report temporal bone procedures in the auditory system that do not have a specific code. Explanation The provider performs a temporal bone procedure on the auditory system using a middle fossa approach that is not represented by any of the standard and active CPT® codes available. Terminology Auditory: Pertaining to the sense of hearing or to the organs of hearing. Middle cranial fossa: The butterfly–shaped depressed area at the base of the cranial cavity where the temporal lobes of the brain and the pituitary glands reside. Temporal bone: A bone on the side of the skull. Tips CPT® guidelines instruct that you should not choose a code that merely approximates the service provided. You should report the service using only the appropriate unlisted procedure code if no such specific procedure or service code exists. You must report a Category III code when available in place of an unlisted procedure code. When reporting a procedure with an unlisted code, submit a cover letter explaining the reason for choosing the unlisted code instead of a defined, active code. Include one or more similar codes, and compare your service to those codes to justify the claim amount you are billing. Also include the operative notes or other relevant documentation to strengthen the claim and to avoid a possible denial. Your payers will consider claims with unlisted procedure codes on a case by case basis, and they will determine payment based on the documentation you provide. Read Less

short_description: Microsurgical techniques, requiring use of operating microscope (List separately in addition to code for primary procedure)
lay_term: Use this code in addition to the code for a primary procedure when the provider uses an operating microscope to facilitate microsurgical techniques involving cutting or suturing. Explanation The provider employs very small instruments and microsurgical techniques to carry out a surgical procedure while viewing the surgical field through an operating microscope. Terminology Loupes: Magnifying lenses attached to glasses or a headband to facilitate microdissection. Tips Knowing payer guidelines is the key to operating microscope reimbursement. Report this code separately in addition to reporting only one primary procedure per operative session, which means that no matter how many times you use the operating microscope while in the OR, you can report 69990 only once, as the code is eligible for reimbursement once per operative session and not per procedure code. Because 69990 is an add–on code, you do not need to append modifier 51, Multiple procedures, with this procedure code. This rule applies even if the provider uses the operating microscope for several procedures during the same session. Therefore, if the provider bills three surgical codes on one date, you can still only bill 69990 once, not three times. If your provider documents in the op note that he used the operating microscope for microsurgery, you must determine whether your payer follows CPT® or CMS guidelines and cross–check the payer's guidelines to see whether it allows you to report the service with 69990. Some payers will provide you with a list of which codes they'll allow with 69990. Key documentation you may find in the op report can include terms such as Weck® scope, Zeiss® scope or Leica®. Do not report 69990 when the provider uses loupes or vision correction. Some procedures include the use of the operating microscope; check the Official Descriptor and do not use this code with those codes. Read Less
